title: Spectroscopic Evidence for Nontrivial Band Topology in Superconducting FeTe/MnTe Heterostructure
summary: FeTe has long been regarded as a nonsuperconducting antiferromagnetic metal with trivial band topology, but recent advances in stoichiometry control have begun to challenge this picture. Here we use higher-order epitaxy on zinc-blende MnTe to stabilize near-stoichiometric FeTe with strongly suppressed interstitial Fe and a superconducting transition onset near 13 K. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals markedly enhanced quasiparticle coherence, well-defined Fe-derived hole bands, and a nearly two-dimensional Dirac-cone-like state near the Fermi level. First-principles calculations identify an inversion between odd- and even-parity bands, yielding nontrivial $Z_2$ topology and a Dirac surface state consistent with experiment. These results elucidate the intrinsic electronic structure of stoichiometric superconducting FeTe and provide evidence for nontrivial band topology, positioning FeTe/MnTe as a promising platform for exploring topological superconductivity.

AI.tldr: Near-stoichiometric FeTe stabilized on MnTe shows superconductivity near 13 K with nontrivial Z2 topology and a Dirac surface state.
AI.motivation: FeTe has traditionally been viewed as a nonsuperconducting antiferromagnetic metal with trivial band topology, but recent stoichiometry-control advances challenge this view. The intrinsic electronic structure of stoichiometric superconducting FeTe and its topological nature remain unresolved.
AI.method: Higher-order epitaxy on zinc-blende MnTe was used to stabilize near-stoichiometric FeTe with strongly suppressed interstitial Fe. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) probed the electronic structure, complemented by first-principles calculations.
AI.result: A superconducting transition onset near 13 K was observed. ARPES revealed enhanced quasiparticle coherence, well-defined Fe-derived hole bands, and a nearly two-dimensional Dirac-cone-like state near the Fermi level. Calculations identified an inversion between odd- and even-parity bands, giving nontrivial Z2 topology and a Dirac surface state consistent with experiment.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify the intrinsic electronic structure of stoichiometric superconducting FeTe and provide evidence for nontrivial band topology, positioning FeTe/MnTe as a promising platform for exploring topological superconductivity.

title: A Different Perspective on Superconductivity in Crystalline Graphene: Exploiting Energetics
summary: A central mystery of crystalline graphene is why superconductivity is so widespread yet often confined to strange slivers near boundaries between distinct isospin-ordered metals. In this paper, we apply a ``two-parent'' energetic framework which we show can explain this unusual form of superconductivity \textit{without} specifying the details of the necessarily present pairing attraction. First-order transitions are crucial here: when two normal isospin-ordered states are degenerate in free energy, even a small net superconducting energy gain may stabilize an equilibrium superconductor. We demonstrate how this is possible even though the small energy gain from pairing is reduced by the expense of reconstructing the normal metal, which is needed to achieve superconducting compatibility. The first order degeneracy also gives superconductivity a choice between two normal state parents, favoring the state with the largest net free energy gain.

AI.tldr: Superconductivity in crystalline graphene is explained via a two-parent energetic framework, where first-order transitions between degenerate isospin-ordered states allow a small pairing gain to stabilize an equilibrium superconductor without specifying the pairing attraction.
AI.motivation: Superconductivity in crystalline graphene is widespread yet typically confined to narrow regions near boundaries between distinct isospin-ordered metals, a puzzling feature. The paper aims to explain this unusual form of superconductivity without needing to specify the details of the pairing attraction.
AI.method: The authors apply a 'two-parent' energetic framework based on first-order transitions. When two normal isospin-ordered states are degenerate in free energy, a small net superconducting energy gain can stabilize an equilibrium superconductor, even accounting for the cost of reconstructing the normal metal required for superconducting compatibility.
AI.result: It is shown to be possible for a small pairing energy gain to stabilize superconductivity despite the reduction from normal-metal reconstruction costs, and the first-order degeneracy lets superconductivity choose between two normal-state parents.
AI.conclusion: The first-order degeneracy favors the parent state with the largest net free energy gain, providing a framework to explain why superconductivity in crystalline graphene appears in slivers near boundaries between isospin-ordered metals.

title: Electronic Reconstruction across the Tilt-Free Transition in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$
summary: The emergence of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in pressurized La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ is intimately linked to a structural transition that suppresses the tilts of the NiO$_6$ octahedra, yet its impact on the electronic structure remains poorly understood. Here, we probe the electronic response across this tilt-free transition at $T_{st}\simeq 544$ K using broadband infrared-to-visible reflectivity at ambient pressure, covering photon energies from 15 meV to 3.2 eV. We observe a pronounced redistribution of spectral weight over an exceptionally broad energy range, with spectral weight transferred from excitations between 1 and 3 eV toward low-energy excitations below 1 eV. Most strikingly, two low-energy interband excitations progressively converge and merge upon entering the tilt-free phase, revealing a substantial reconstruction of the finite-energy electronic structure. These changes point to a reconstruction of the bilayer Ni $3d_{z^2}$-derived electronic states, whose interlayer coupling is central to proposed mechanisms of superconductivity in La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$. Our results establish the tilt-free transition as a direct route to reorganizing the electronic degrees of freedom implicated in high-$T_c$ superconductivity and provide an ambient-pressure reference for the electronic structure of the superconducting state.

AI.tldr: Broadband infrared-to-visible reflectivity on La₃Ni₂O₇ at ambient pressure reveals that the tilt-free structural transition at ~544 K drives a broad spectral-weight redistribution and merges two low-energy interband excitations, indicating reconstruction of bilayer Ni 3d_z² states tied to superconductivity.
AI.motivation: High-Tc superconductivity in pressurized La₃Ni₂O₇ is linked to a structural transition that suppresses NiO₆ octahedral tilts, but how this tilt-free transition affects the electronic structure is poorly understood. Clarifying this link is important because interlayer coupling of Ni 3d_z² states is central to proposed superconductivity mechanisms.

AI.result: A pronounced spectral-weight redistribution occurs over an exceptionally broad energy range, with weight transferred from 1–3 eV excitations toward low-energy excitations below 1 eV. Two low-energy interband excitations progressively converge and merge upon entering the tilt-free phase, revealing substantial reconstruction of the finite-energy electronic structure.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate reconstruction of bilayer Ni 3d_z²-derived electronic states, establishing the tilt-free transition as a direct route to reorganizing electronic degrees of freedom implicated in high-Tc superconductivity and providing an ambient-pressure reference for the electronic structure of the superconducting state.

title: Fingerprints of unconventional pairing in superconductor-hole-gas heterostructures
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 7 pages, 2 figures
summary: Superconductor and two-dimensional hole gas heterostructures are promising platforms for quantum devices, but their intrinsic properties, e.g., unconventional pairings, are hard to access experimentally. Here, we show that the in-plane-field dependence of the superfluid stiffness and spin susceptibility exhibits nonanalyticities encoding the induced gap structure in the hole gas. Additionally, Fourier harmonics of the stiffness tensor's field-angle dependence, accessible via kinetic-inductance measurements, provide fingerprints of unconventional pairing and cubic Rashba coupling.

AI.tldr: The in-plane magnetic-field dependence of superfluid stiffness and spin susceptibility in superconductor/two-dimensional-hole-gas heterostructures shows nonanalyticities that encode the induced pairing gap, and Fourier harmonics of the field-angle-dependent stiffness tensor provide fingerprints of unconventional pairing and cubic Rashba coupling.
AI.motivation: Superconductor/2D hole gas heterostructures are promising for quantum devices, but their intrinsic properties (e.g., unconventional pairings) are difficult to access experimentally, motivating a measurable probe of the induced gap structure.
AI.method: The authors analyze the in-plane-field dependence of the superfluid stiffness and spin susceptibility of the proximitized hole gas, examining nonanalyticities and the field-angle dependence of the stiffness tensor; kinetic-inductance measurements are proposed to access the Fourier harmonics.
AI.result: The superfluid stiffness and spin susceptibility exhibit nonanalyticities as functions of in-plane field that encode the induced gap structure, and the Fourier harmonics of the stiffness tensor's field-angle dependence serve as fingerprints distinguishing unconventional pairing and cubic Rashba coupling.
AI.conclusion: Kinetic-inductance measurements of the field-angle-dependent stiffness tensor provide a practical fingerprint of unconventional pairing and cubic Rashba coupling in superconductor/2D hole gas heterostructures.

title: Continuous Event Weighting for Resonance Searches
summary: We develop a continuous event weighting framework for resonance searches that uses auxiliary event information without dividing the data into increasingly fine sensitivity categories. A hard selection is a binary weight, finite categories correspond to piecewise constant weights, and in the background dominated limit their fine partition approaches a continuous signal to background density ratio weight. The construction retains auxiliary discrimination in a single physically interpretable resonance spectrum, with calculable statistical variance and direct recovery of the selected signal yield. One million fully explicit event level pseudoexperiments using Gaussian, Gamma, and Beta auxiliary observables verify yield recovery, uncertainty propagation, and frequentist coverage while substantially improving discovery sensitivity. The method is further tested on publicly available CMS Run2016G and Run2016H diphoton Open Data as an independent real data benchmark, using detector level gluon fusion Higgs simulation only as the signal reference. This is a methodological test of the framework, not a CMS Higgs analysis. The results demonstrate a practical route to exploiting continuous auxiliary information without proliferating sensitivity driven event categories.

AI.tldr: A continuous event weighting framework for resonance searches encodes auxiliary event information as a continuous signal-to-background density ratio weight, avoiding fine event categories while improving discovery sensitivity and preserving statistically interpretable variance.
AI.motivation: Conventional resonance searches either apply hard selections (binary weights) or split data into increasingly fine sensitivity categories (piecewise constant weights), which proliferates categories and complicates statistical interpretation. The authors seek a way to retain auxiliary discrimination in a single interpretable spectrum without fragmenting the dataset.
AI.method: The framework generalizes hard selection and finite category binning: hard cuts are binary weights, finite categories are piecewise constant weights, and in the background-dominated limit a fine partition approaches a continuous signal-to-background density ratio weight. Auxiliary discrimination is folded into one physically interpretable resonance spectrum with calculable statistical variance and direct recovery of selected signal yield. Validation uses one million fully explicit event-level pseudoexperiments with Gaussian, Gamma, and Beta auxiliary observables, plus publicly available CMS Run2016G/Run2016H diphoton Open Data as an independent benchmark, with detector-level gluon fusion Higgs simulation used only as signal reference.
AI.result: Pseudoexperiments verify yield recovery, uncertainty propagation, and frequentist coverage while substantially improving discovery sensitivity. The CMS Open Data benchmark provides an independent real-data test of the method.
AI.conclusion: Continuous auxiliary information can be exploited without proliferating sensitivity-driven event categories, offering a practical and statistically well-behaved route for resonance searches. The CMS study is a methodological test, not a CMS Higgs analysis.

title: The Ganglion Network Model: Evolving Trapped Phases in Porous Media
summary: Partially miscible ganglia trapped within porous media, spanning one or multiple pores and evolving through diffusive mass transfer, are common in subsurface (e.g., CO$_2$ and H$_2$ storage) and manufacturing (e.g., fuel cells) applications. We present the ganglion network model (GNM), a reduced-order method for simulating how a population of such ganglia evolves inside an arbitrary porous microstructure. GNM operates on a tree graph, the ganglion network, extracted from the pore-scale image of a given sample. Each point on the graph encodes a possible ganglion configuration in the void space, without any loss of geometric or topological complexity. The evolution of a population is modeled by representing each ganglion as a particle on the graph and tracking it according to a set of rules formulated herein. The rules capture capillary events such as pore invasion, retraction, snap-off, fragmentation, and merger. Unlike pore-network models, another graph-based modeling tool at the pore scale, GNM solves no system of equations and its cost scales with ganglion count, not domain size. We validate GNM against an image-based pore-network model in 2.5D and 3D domains with populations undergoing ripening, dissolution, and growth. We find good agreement in ganglion statistics, aggregate properties, and spatial configuration. We further argue that the ganglion network is the statistical space needed for extending kinetic theories of Ostwald ripening from single- to multi-pore ganglia, and provide an outline for how to do this. GNM opens the door to modeling other dynamics of trapped phases in porous media.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the ganglion network model (GNM), a reduced-order, equation-free method that simulates the diffusive evolution (ripening, dissolution, growth) of populations of multiphase ganglia in arbitrary porous microstructures by tracking ganglia as particles on a tree graph extracted from pore-scale images.
AI.motivation: Partially miscible ganglia trapped in porous media, spanning one or multiple pores and evolving via diffusive mass transfer, are ubiquitous in subsurface applications (CO2 and H2 storage) and manufacturing (fuel cells). Existing pore-scale tools, notably pore-network models, require solving systems of equations whose cost scales with domain size, making large populations of ganglia expensive to simulate. A reduced-order approach that captures full geometric and topological complexity while scaling with ganglion count rather than domain size is needed.
AI.method: GNM operates on a tree graph—the ganglion network—extracted from the pore-scale image of a given sample. Each point on the graph encodes a possible ganglion configuration in the void space without loss of geometric or topological complexity. Each ganglion is represented as a particle on the graph and tracked by a set of rules capturing capillary events: pore invasion, retraction, snap-off, fragmentation, and merger. Crucially, GNM solves no system of equations, and its computational cost scales with ganglion count rather than domain size.
AI.result: GNM is validated against an image-based pore-network model in 2.5D and 3D domains for populations undergoing ripening, dissolution, and growth. The authors find good agreement in ganglion statistics, aggregate properties, and spatial configuration.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that the ganglion network constitutes the statistical space needed to extend kinetic theories of Ostwald ripening from single-pore to multi-pore ganglia, and outline how to achieve this extension. GNM opens the door to modeling other dynamics of trapped phases in porous media.

title: Reference-Measure Freedom of the Effective Hamiltonian: From Stochastic Thermodynamics to the Macroscopic Limit
summary: The effective Hamiltonian (EH), also referred to as the potential of mean force or free-energy landscape, is widely used to describe equilibrium properties and slow dynamics in chemical and softmatter systems. However, the conventional EH has been argued to be ill-defined because it does not transform as a scalar under a change of coordinates. Here, we show that this apparent problem originates from an implicit change of the reference measure (gauge) with respect to which the equilibrium probability density is defined. We formulate the equilibrium measure and the Fokker--Planck equation (FPE) intrinsically on the manifold of slow variables and show that an EH is a scalar function defined with respect to a chosen gauge. Different EHs, including the conventional EH and the diffusion-dependent EH recently proposed in a Riemannian formulation, thus provide different gauge representations of the same intrinsic equilibrium measure and stochastic dynamics. We further show that the gauge choice has an operational meaning: different restraint protocols for the slow variables select different reference measures. Finally, when the equilibrium measure obeys a large-deviation principle in a macroscopic limit, differences among EHs associated with subleading gauges become subleading relative to the large-deviation speed. The leading part of the EH is then determined by the gauge-independent large-deviation rate function, and the corresponding deterministic dynamics is likewise gauge independent.

AI.tldr: The effective Hamiltonian's apparent coordinate-dependence arises from an implicit change of the reference measure (gauge); EHs are scalar functions defined relative to a chosen gauge, and different EH formulations are gauge representations of the same intrinsic equilibrium measure and stochastic dynamics.
AI.motivation: The conventional effective Hamiltonian (EH) is widely used to describe equilibrium and slow dynamics in chemical and soft-matter systems, but has been criticized as ill-defined because it does not transform as a scalar under coordinate changes. This paper aims to resolve this apparent inconsistency.
AI.method: The authors formulate the equilibrium measure and the Fokker–Planck equation intrinsically on the manifold of slow variables, and introduce a gauge (reference measure) with respect to which the EH is defined as a scalar function. They compare different EHs, including the conventional EH and a diffusion-dependent Riemannian EH, as distinct gauge representations. They also link gauge choice to restraint protocols, and analyze the large-deviation limit where subleading gauges become negligible.
AI.result: The apparent non-scalar behavior of the conventional EH is traced to an implicit change of reference measure. Different EHs (conventional, diffusion-dependent Riemannian) represent the same intrinsic equilibrium measure and stochastic dynamics under different gauges. Gauge choice has operational meaning: different restraint protocols select different reference measures. In the macroscopic large-deviation limit, differences among EHs from subleading gauges become subleading relative to the large-deviation speed.
AI.conclusion: The EH's coordinate-dependence is a gauge artifact, not an inconsistency. The leading part of the EH is determined by the gauge-independent large-deviation rate function, and the corresponding deterministic dynamics is also gauge independent, providing a rigorous intrinsic foundation for effective Hamiltonians.

title: Accidental accuracy and formal consistency in $GW$+BSE: Exact benchmarks and regime-dependent error cancellation
summary: Standard many-body perturbation theory for optical excitations combines the $GW$ approximation for quasiparticle energies with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for the electron-hole response. Formally, the BSE kernel must equal the functional derivative of the self-energy, $K=δΣ/δG$. In routine practice, however, the kernel is built from a statically screened direct interaction and a bare exchange interaction, which breaks this consistency. Using exact diagonalization of the extended Hubbard dimer, we construct a controlled benchmark that isolates the price of this inconsistency. We show that the internally inconsistent practical $GW$+BSE construction frequently yields accurate optical gaps through accidental cancellation between an underestimated $GW$ gap and an oversized bare-exchange kernel, and we map the regions of parameter space where this accidental accuracy occurs. Upon switching on the nearest-neighbor interaction and binding the exciton, the practical construction remains the accurate one throughout the weak-binding regime, with cancellation optima at parts in $10^{3}$, while the frozen-$W$ construction fails at every binding strength. Beyond a binding threshold both static constructions deteriorate, showing that deeply bound excitons require physics beyond any static kernel. Accidental accuracy is therefore a property of the weak-binding regime, and the systematic failure of the frozen-$W$ derivative kernel within the explored parameter space traces to its overscreening of the exchange channel. The accuracy of the practical kernel is an accidental cancellation of two independent errors, an underestimated quasiparticle gap and an oversized exchange term, not a hidden consistency. These results provide a controlled taxonomy of approximation failure in $GW$+BSE and a precise diagnostic for when standard workflows can be trusted.

AI.tldr: Using exact diagonalization of the extended Hubbard dimer, the authors show that the practical $GW$+BSE kernel's accuracy is an accidental cancellation between an underestimated $GW$ quasiparticle gap and an oversized bare-exchange term, valid only in the weak-binding regime, while static kernels fail for deeply bound excitons.
AI.motivation: Standard $GW$+BSE practice violates the formal consistency condition that the BSE kernel equals the self-energy functional derivative ($K=δΣ/δG$), instead using a statically screened direct interaction plus bare exchange. The paper aims to isolate and quantify the price of this internal inconsistency and determine when standard workflows can be trusted.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of the extended Hubbard dimer is used to build a controlled benchmark isolating the inconsistency. The authors compare the practical $GW$+BSE construction against a frozen-$W$ derivative-based kernel, map parameter regions where accidental accuracy occurs, and systematically vary nearest-neighbor interaction to drive exciton binding across weak- to strong-binding regimes.
AI.result: The practical $GW$+BSE construction frequently yields accurate optical gaps via accidental cancellation between an underestimated $GW$ gap and an oversized bare-exchange kernel. In the weak-binding regime it stays accurate with cancellation optima at parts in $10^{3}$, while the frozen-$W$ construction fails at every binding strength. Beyond a binding threshold, both static constructions deteriorate, indicating deeply bound excitons require physics beyond any static kernel. The frozen-$W$ failure traces to overscreening of the exchange channel.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy of the practical kernel is an accidental cancellation of two independent errors—an underestimated quasiparticle gap and an oversized exchange term—not a hidden consistency. The work provides a controlled taxonomy of approximation failure in $GW$+BSE and a precise diagnostic for when standard workflows can be trusted.

title: Theory of criticality-enabled $U(1)$ symmetry breaking in a class of 1+1D systems
summary: We present an analytic theory of the recently proposed phenomenon of spontaneous $U(1)$ symmetry breaking at 1+1D Lifshitz quantum critical points. The low-energy field theory contains two periodic scalars $θ$ and $φ$, with a Berry phase coupling that makes $θ$ canonically conjugate to the $U(1)$ charge density $\partial_x φ$. Within a controlled large-$N$ limit, we demonstrate that the $U(1)$-charged phase vertex $e^{iβθ}$ develops long-range order, while the conjugate vertex $e^{iβφ}$ decays as a stretched exponential, $\log\langle e^{iβφ(x)} e^{-iβφ(0)}\rangle\propto-|β|^{4/3}|x|^{2/3}$. Going beyond the large-$N$ limit, we give an analytic argument that the Lifshitz field theory supports $U(1)$ long-range order provided its dynamical exponent satisfies $z\neq1$, a condition strongly supported by existing calculations. We test these predictions using finite-size and infinite-system DMRG in an itinerant-fermion chain with $U(1) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. At the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ ferromagnetic transition, the spin sector of the chain maps to the Lifshitz field theory. Consistent with analytic predictions, the $U(1)$-charged spin-nematic bond operator $S_i^+S_{i+1}^+$ exhibits long-range order, while the electron Green's function shows stretched-exponential decay. Together, these results elucidate the mechanism and consequences of criticality-enabled $U(1)$ symmetry breaking in 1+1D.

AI.tldr: An analytic theory is developed for spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking at 1+1D Lifshitz quantum critical points, showing U(1)-charged long-range order coexisting with stretched-exponential decay of a conjugate vertex, confirmed by DMRG in an itinerant-fermion chain.
AI.motivation: The recently proposed phenomenon of spontaneous U(1) symmetry breaking at 1+1D Lifshitz quantum critical points lacks a clear analytic understanding of its mechanism and consequences. The paper aims to explain why criticality enables U(1) symmetry breaking and to characterize the resulting order and correlations.
AI.method: The low-energy field theory of two periodic scalars θ and φ is studied, with a Berry phase coupling making θ canonically conjugate to the U(1) charge density ∂_x φ. The authors analyze it within a controlled large-N limit and give a general analytic argument for U(1) long-range order when the dynamical exponent satisfies z≠1. Predictions are tested with finite-size and infinite-system DMRG on an itinerant-fermion chain with U(1)⋊Z_2 symmetry, where the spin sector at the Z_2 ferromagnetic transition maps to the Lifshitz field theory.
AI.result: In the large-N limit, the U(1)-charged phase vertex e^{iβθ} develops long-range order, while the conjugate vertex e^{iβφ} decays as a stretched exponential with log⟨e^{iβφ(x)}e^{-iβφ(0)}⟩ ∝ -|β|^{4/3}|x|^{2/3}. The theory supports U(1) long-range order provided z≠1. DMRG confirms that the U(1)-charged spin-nematic bond operator S_i^+ S_{i+1}^+ exhibits long-range order, while the electron Green's function shows stretched-exponential decay.
AI.conclusion: These results elucidate the mechanism and consequences of criticality-enabled U(1) symmetry breaking in 1+1D, with analytic predictions corroborated by numerical DMRG simulations in an itinerant-fermion chain.

title: A Machine-Learned Interatomic Potential Free-Energy Surface for the First Step of MIL-101(Cr) Secondary Building Unit Formation
summary: Metal-organic framework (MOF) self-assembly mechanisms remain poorly characterized because ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) are accurate but too computationally expensive to converge the free-energy surfaces (FES) that govern secondary building unit (SBU) nucleation and growth. This work addresses that limitation for the first step of MIL-101(Cr) SBU formation. Using MACE-POLAR-M, a long-range-aware equivariant machine-learned interatomic potential fine-tuned on a compact DFT reference dataset built from exploratory metadynamics, this work obtains a converged 2D FES for this step at a level of theory (ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPP) at which AIMD would be prohibitively expensive. The pre-trained model samples relevant configurations but gets the thermodynamics wrong, predicting an endothermic reaction and a false global minimum. Fine-tuning corrects both, recovering the expected exothermic process and the correct product basin in agreement with proposed literature mechanisms. The resulting FES also refines the mechanism. It shows that water release from the chromium center proceeds stepwise, through two sequential energy barriers, rather than the single concerted step originally proposed. We find that model accuracy is specific to the reaction coordinate and does not extend to the dissociated fragment configurations excluded from fine-tuning, a direct consequence of the training-data choice that protects accuracy along the reaction path for the FES prediction task. Together, these results establish a validated, computationally tractable route to obtain free-energy surfaces for MOF formation chemistry, transferable to other reactions where AIMD remains prohibitive, and identify training-data composition as the key determinant of which reaction properties a fine-tuned checkpoint can reliably describe.

AI.tldr: A long-range-aware equivariant MLIP (MACE-POLAR-M), fine-tuned on a compact DFT dataset from metadynamics, yields a converged 2D free-energy surface for the first step of MIL-101(Cr) SBU formation at ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPP accuracy, where AIMD would be prohibitive. Fine-tuning corrects the pre-trained model's erroneous thermodynamics and reveals a stepwise, two-barrier water-release mechanism.

Model accuracy is probed along versus off the reaction coordinate.

Fine-tuning recovers the expected exothermic process and the correct product basin, consistent with proposed literature mechanisms. The FES shows water release from the chromium center is stepwise, involving two sequential energy barriers rather than a single concerted step. title: Synchronous Monte Carlo method and its application to a mean-field spin glass model
summary: Standard Markov chain Monte Carlo methods update variables one at a time to satisfy detailed balance, which prevents them from fully exploiting massively parallel hardware such as graphics processing units (GPUs). We study a Monte Carlo method for systems with pairwise interactions in which all variables are updated simultaneously, made possible by auxiliary Gaussian fields introduced through the Gaussian integral identity. The method satisfies detailed balance and is therefore guaranteed to converge to the canonical distribution. For mean-field spin glasses, its dynamics can be analyzed exactly by dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). Applying the method and the DMFT to the random orthogonal model, which exhibits a random first-order transition, we find that the fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is clearly violated below the dynamical transition temperature, and that the relation between response and correlation takes the two-slope form of a generalized FDT, with simulations and theory in quantitative agreement.

AI.tldr: A parallel Monte Carlo method with simultaneous variable updates is shown to satisfy detailed balance and converge to the canonical distribution; for mean-field spin glasses its dynamics is solved exactly via DMFT, revealing a clear violation of the FDT below the dynamical transition with a two-slope generalized FDT.
AI.motivation: Standard Markov chain Monte Carlo updates variables one at a time to satisfy detailed balance, which prevents full exploitation of massively parallel hardware such as GPUs. This motivates a method enabling simultaneous updates of all variables.
AI.method: The authors study a Monte Carlo method for systems with pairwise interactions in which all variables are updated simultaneously, enabled by auxiliary Gaussian fields introduced through the Gaussian integral identity. The method satisfies detailed balance so it is guaranteed to converge to the canonical distribution. For mean-field spin glasses, its dynamics is analyzed exactly using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT).
AI.result: Applying the method and DMFT to the random orthogonal model, which exhibits a random first-order transition, shows that the fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) is clearly violated below the dynamical transition temperature. The relation between response and correlation takes the two-slope form of a generalized FDT, with simulations and theory in quantitative agreement.
AI.conclusion: A simultaneous-update Monte Carlo scheme satisfying detailed balance exploits parallel hardware while preserving correct canonical sampling, and its exact DMFT analysis of mean-field spin glasses reveals a two-slope generalized FDT emerging from FDT violation below the dynamical transition.

title: Radiative Data for As III, Se III, Hf IV, and Tl IV: HFR and MCDHF Calculations for Hot Subdwarf Spectroscopy
summary: Accurate oscillator strengths for doubly and triply ionised heavy elements are required for quantitative spectroscopy of hot subdwarfs, but available data remain sparse. We present new radiative data for As III, Se III, Hf IV and Tl IV, calculated with the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method including core-polarization effects and semi-empirical adjustment of radial parameters to experimental energy levels. Independent multiconfiguration Dirac-Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) computations were also performed for As III, Hf IV and Tl IV, while published MCDHF data were adopted for Se III to assess the reliability of the HFR oscillator strengths. The largest discrepancies between the two approaches are mainly associated with weak transitions, strong cancellation effects, or significant gauge disagreement. For strong transitions satisfying the adopted reliability criteria, we found a good agreement between the oscillator strengths obtained by both methods. The new data have already been applied to the spectra of the heavy-metal hot subdwarfs LS IV-14$^\circ$116 and EC 22536-5304, enabling abundance determinations for As, Se, Hf, and Tl and providing additional lines for future spectroscopic studies.

AI.tldr: New accurate oscillator strengths for As III, Se III, Hf IV, and Tl IV are computed using HFR and MCDHF methods, showing good agreement for strong transitions, and are applied to abundance determinations in heavy-metal hot subdwarfs LS IV-14°116 and EC 22536-5304.
AI.motivation: Quantitative spectroscopy of hot subdwarfs requires accurate oscillator strengths for doubly and triply ionised heavy elements, but such radiative data remain sparse.
AI.method: Radiative data were computed with the pseudo-relativistic Hartree-Fock (HFR) method including core-polarization effects and semi-empirical adjustment of radial parameters to experimental energy levels. Independent multiconfiguration Dirac-Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) computations were performed for As III, Hf IV, and Tl IV, while published MCDHF data were adopted for Se III to cross-check the HFR oscillator strengths.
AI.result: The largest discrepancies between HFR and MCDHF arise from weak transitions, strong cancellation effects, or significant gauge disagreement. For strong transitions meeting the reliability criteria, good agreement was found between the oscillator strengths from both methods. The data enabled abundance determinations for As, Se, Hf, and Tl in the heavy-metal hot subdwarfs LS IV-14°116 and EC 22536-5304.
AI.conclusion: The new oscillator strengths provide reliable radiative data and additional spectral lines for future spectroscopic studies of hot subdwarfs, with HFR and MCDHF agreeing well for strong transitions.

title: Self-verifying time-resolved multicomponent gas analysis from raw sensor signals
summary: Gas sensor arrays can estimate the composition of gas mixtures from their response patterns. However, when a sensor is used outside the laboratory, the true gas concentrations are unknown, so there is usually no direct way to determine whether the estimated result is reliable. Here, we develop a physics-constrained neural network that estimates time-varying gas concentrations and reconstructs the corresponding sensor signals at the same time. We tested the method with a twelve-channel membrane-type surface stress sensor array exposed to water-ethanol mixtures whose concentrations changed over time. The model reconstructed the concentration profiles of both components from the raw signals. Artificial offsets and sensitivity changes in one channel were detected from disagreement between the measured and reconstructed signals. This work aims to enable reliable, self-verifying operation without ground-truth reference.

Validation uses a twelve-channel membrane-type surface stress sensor (MSS) array exposed to water-ethanol mixtures with time-varying concentrations; the model reconstructs concentration profiles of both components from raw signals.

Anomalies were detected via consistency checks: artificial offsets and sensitivity changes in one channel were flagged from disagreement between measured and reconstructed signals, while deletion or replacement of part of a measurement record was detected from violations of the sorption and mechanical equations.

title: Hidden Angular Momentum Loop Currents in Symmetric Crystals
summary: Loop-current order has been invoked to explain unconventional electronic phases, with the crystal lattice usually regarded as a passive host for the underlying collective dynamics. Here we show that circulating currents can originate in the lattice itself, sustained by quantum and thermal fluctuations. We develop a microscopic description of angular momentum exchange that separates transfer between sites from crystalline restoring torques and reveals how circulation can emerge in a symmetry-preserving equilibrium state. In a two-dimensional elastic lattice preserving time-reversal, inversion, and fourfold rotational symmetries, we uncover opposite current loops on neighboring plaquettes while the mean angular momentum vanishes at every site. These currents are sustained by zero-point fluctuations in the phonon vacuum and persist at finite temperature. We trace their origin to directional elastic interactions in locally symmetry-lowered environments, with the higher crystal symmetry organizing the resulting currents into a compensated pattern of circulation. Our results extend the physics of equilibrium loop currents to lattice dynamics, revealing that elastic geometry can organize fluctuations into persistent angular momentum circulation without electronic or magnetic order, external driving, or spontaneous symmetry breaking.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that persistent loop currents can emerge purely from lattice dynamics—sustained by zero-point and thermal fluctuations in a symmetric elastic lattice—without electronic/magnetic order or symmetry breaking.
AI.motivation: Loop-current order is typically attributed to electronic collective dynamics, with the crystal lattice treated as a passive background. The authors question whether circulating currents can originate intrinsically in the lattice itself.
AI.method: A microscopic description of angular momentum exchange is developed, separating inter-site transfer from crystalline restoring torques. A two-dimensional elastic lattice preserving time-reversal, inversion, and fourfold rotational symmetry is analyzed, with directional elastic interactions in locally symmetry-lowered environments.
AI.result: Opposite current loops appear on neighboring plaquettes while mean angular momentum vanishes at every site. The currents are sustained by phonon zero-point fluctuations and persist at finite temperature, forming a compensated circulation pattern organized by the higher crystal symmetry.
AI.conclusion: Equilibrium loop currents are extended to lattice dynamics: elastic geometry alone can organize fluctuations into persistent angular momentum circulation without electronic or magnetic order, external driving, or spontaneous symmetry breaking.

title: Resonances control when multiterminal Josephson currents reduce to two-terminal couplings
comment: 42 pages (12-page main text plus Supplemental Material), 20 figures, 11 tables
summary: Multiterminal Josephson junctions, in which one weak link couples three or more superconductors, are studied as hosts of topological Andreev bands, multi-pair supercurrents and tunable circuit elements. Their currents are modeled both as pairwise networks of two-terminal couplings and through genuinely multiterminal processes such as quartets. We ask how accurate the pairwise description is and what controls its error. In a microscopic scattering model of planar junctions, we compare exact currents with the best pairwise approximation, which allows arbitrary nonsinusoidal couplings. In ensembles of disordered three- and four-terminal junctions, the pairwise terms capture nearly all of the energy variation, yet the median current error ranges from 8.0 to 21.2 percent, about twice the energy error, because currents weigh the multiterminal harmonics more strongly. Designed devices extend the comparison to sixteen terminals. We identify a mechanism that controls this error. A normal-region mode near the Fermi level that couples to three or more terminals produces large nonpairwise currents, and detuning it with a gate suppresses them. Shifting only this mode, selected from normal-state properties, predicts the gate dependence of the error in eight three- and four-terminal devices without fitting currents. Finite-gap calculations in two clean devices confirm a drop from tens of percent near resonance to below one percent. An analytic single-level model gives a sufficient detuning for pairwise accuracy at any terminal count. Planar junctions thus inherit the resonant and cotunneling regimes known from quantum dots, and normal-state properties identify the mode that selects between them.

AI.tldr: This work quantifies the accuracy of pairwise (two-terminal) approximations versus exact currents in multiterminal Josephson junctions and identifies the microscopic mechanism controlling the error: a near-Fermi-level normal-region mode coupling to multiple terminals.
AI.motivation: Multiterminal Josephson junctions host topological Andreev bands, multi-pair supercurrents, and tunable circuit elements, and their currents are often modeled either as pairwise networks of two-terminal couplings or through genuinely multiterminal processes (e.g., quartets). It is unclear how accurate the pairwise description is and what governs its error.
AI.method: Using a microscopic scattering model of planar junctions, the authors compare exact currents with the best pairwise approximation (allowing arbitrary nonsinusoidal couplings) in ensembles of disordered three- and four-terminal junctions, and extend the comparison to designed sixteen-terminal devices. They identify a controlling mechanism via a normal-region mode near the Fermi level coupling to three or more terminals, and test it by gate detuning. An analytic single-level model is derived to give a sufficient detuning for pairwise accuracy at any terminal count.

title: A State-Transition Information Space for Time-Series Dynamics: Theory and Application
summary: Characterizing dynamical organization in time series requires distinguishing the diversity of accessible states from uncertainty in their temporal transitions. Here we introduce a state-transition information space based on two normalized entropy measures derived from ordinal patterns: K_q, quantifying ordinal-state diversity, and K_t, quantifying transition uncertainty. Their joint K_t-K_q representation provides a two-dimensional framework in which dynamical regimes and their temporal evolution can be examined. Theoretical properties establish the bounded relation 0 <= K_t <= K_q <= 1, while canonical time series identify distinct empirical domains ranging from ordered dynamics to near-maximal randomness. Sliding-window analysis further shows that systems can exhibit temporal trajectories through the K_t-K_q plane rather than remaining at a fixed dynamical state. Application to 1,879 monthly naturalized streamflow records from the U.S. rivers shows that river dynamics occupy a distinct intermediate region between ordered and highly disordered regimes. Moreover, river positions shift systematically toward higher K_t and K_q with increasing drainage area, revealing scale-dependent organization of streamflow dynamics. The framework therefore provides a compact means of comparing state diversity, transition uncertainty, and their temporal and spatial organization across time-series systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-dimensional "state-transition information space" built from two normalized ordinal-pattern entropies (K_q for state diversity, K_t for transition uncertainty) to characterize dynamical organization in time series, and applies it to 1,879 U.S. streamflow records.
AI.motivation: Characterizing dynamical organization in time series requires separating two distinct aspects: the diversity of accessible states and the uncertainty in their temporal transitions. Existing single-measure approaches conflate these, so a framework that jointly and compactly captures both is needed.
AI.method: The authors construct a state-transition information space from ordinal patterns using two normalized entropy measures: K_q (ordinal-state diversity) and K_t (transition uncertainty). The joint K_t–K_q representation defines a 2D framework for examining dynamical regimes and their evolution. They establish theoretical bounds, benchmark the space with canonical time series, and use sliding-window analysis to track temporal trajectories. They apply the framework to 1,879 monthly naturalized streamflow records from U.S. rivers and relate positions in the space to drainage area.

Sliding-window analysis shows systems move along trajectories in the K_t–K_q plane rather than occupying a fixed state. River dynamics occupy a distinct intermediate region between ordered and highly disordered regimes, and shift systematically toward higher K_t and K_q as drainage area increases.
AI.conclusion: The K_t–K_q information space provides a compact, general means of comparing state diversity, transition uncertainty, and their temporal and spatial organization across time-series systems, revealing scale-dependent organization in streamflow dynamics.

title: A Variance-Decomposition Formula for Direct and Adjoint Monte Carlo Particle Transport Problems
summary: In fixed-source Monte Carlo particle-transport problems, obtaining an acceptable variance on the sought response is of paramount importance. Currently, the only rigorous tool to analyze the variance of such games is the framework of the moment equations, which is unfortunately unwieldy to use in practice. In this paper, we establish a formula that enables expressing the variance of a Monte Carlo simulation as a sum of 'variance contributions' collected throughout the underlying particletransport process. This formula applies to both direct and adjoint games, and provides a new tool to pinpoint the variance-inducing mechanisms in Monte Carlo simulations, understand common variance-reduction techniques, and even conceive new ones. We showcase the use of the variance-decomposition formula on several applications. In particular, we revisit zero-variance schemes and analyze existing variance-reduction techniques, underlining their strengths and weaknesses. A few relevant numerical examples substantiate our theoretical findings.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a variance-decomposition formula expressing the variance of fixed-source Monte Carlo particle-transport simulations as a sum of contributions collected along the transport process, applicable to both direct and adjoint games, and uses it to analyze variance-reduction techniques.
AI.motivation: Obtaining an acceptable variance on the sought response is critical in fixed-source Monte Carlo transport. The only rigorous existing tool, the moment-equations framework, is unwieldy to use in practice, motivating a more tractable approach to analyze and understand simulation variance.
AI.method: The authors establish a variance-decomposition formula that expresses the Monte Carlo simulation variance as a sum of 'variance contributions' accumulated throughout the underlying particle-transport process. The formula applies to both direct and adjoint games.
AI.result: The formula provides a new tool to pinpoint variance-inducing mechanisms, understand common variance-reduction techniques, and conceive new ones. It is showcased on several applications, including revisiting zero-variance schemes and analyzing existing variance-reduction techniques with their strengths and weaknesses, substantiated by relevant numerical examples.
AI.conclusion: The variance-decomposition formula offers a practical alternative to the moment-equations framework, enabling systematic analysis and potentially the conception of new variance-reduction techniques in Monte Carlo particle transport.

title: Interdependent-Network Criticality without a Second Network: Cascading Collapse of the Joule-Coupled Insulator-Metal Transition in $VO_2$
comment: Main article pages 1-14 pages Supplementary Material pages 15-26
summary: When driven by a large enough electric field or current, the insulating state of vanadium dioxide ($VO_2$) typically collapses abruptly into the metallic state (the insulator-metal transition, IMT) following a brief incubation delay. These incubation delays, typically lasting microseconds or less, have been analyzed predominantly through macroscopic electro-thermal modeling, providing little statistical insight into the transition dynamics. Here, we investigate the electrically driven IMT in a two-dimensional $VO_2$ lattice and demonstrate that the material behaves as a complex, interdependent network despite being a single structural entity. Because metallic domains dissipate significantly more Joule heat than insulating regions, each switching event raises the Joule heating of the network, resulting in network dependency and triggering a cascading chain reaction. Combining time-resolved resistance measurements with a Joule-coupled resistor-network model and interdependent-network theory, we observe an abrupt (first-order) transition preceded by an anomalously long incubation plateau lasting thousands of seconds. During this metastable plateau, an effective branching factor of the switching activity approaches unity at criticality, and the plateau lifetime diverges with exponent $ζ=1/2$; the order parameter scales with exponent $β=1/2$. These signatures coincide with those predicted for interdependent networks, indicating that dissipative Joule coupling alone can drive mixed-order catastrophic cascades in a single-network correlated-oxide system.

AI.tldr: Electrically driven insulator-metal transition in a 2D VO2 lattice is shown to behave as an interdependent network, exhibiting an anomalously long incubation plateau and mixed-order critical signatures consistent with interdependent-network theory.
AI.motivation: Incubation delays preceding the electrically driven insulator-metal transition in VO2 are typically microseconds or shorter and have been studied mainly via macroscopic electro-thermal modeling, which offers little statistical insight into the transition dynamics. The authors aim to uncover the statistical and collective mechanisms governing these delays.
AI.method: The study investigates electrically driven IMT in a two-dimensional VO2 lattice, treating it as a complex interdependent network. Metallic domains dissipate more Joule heat than insulating regions, so each switching event raises network Joule heating, creating network dependency and cascading. Time-resolved resistance measurements are combined with a Joule-coupled resistor-network model and interdependent-network theory.
AI.result: An abrupt first-order transition is observed, preceded by an anomalously long incubation plateau lasting thousands of seconds. During this metastable plateau, the effective branching factor of switching activity approaches unity at criticality; the plateau lifetime diverges with exponent ζ=1/2, and the order parameter scales with exponent β=1/2. These signatures match predictions for interdependent networks.
AI.conclusion: Dissipative Joule coupling alone can drive mixed-order catastrophic cascades in a single-network correlated-oxide system, demonstrating that a single structural entity (VO2) can behave as an interdependent network subject to cascading transitions.

title: Energy-Efficient Non-Volatile Photonic Switching via Composition-Engineered Sn-Doped GST
summary: Integrated phase-change photonics allows non-volatile optical switching with no static power draw, but the electrical energy needed to reversibly switch the material's state limits practical scaling. Efforts to improve energy efficiency have mostly focused on device optimization, such as redesigning the integrated microheater or waveguide. Here, we take a different, materials-centered approach by alloying Sn to Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ (GST) without altering the device structure or CMOS compatibility. We explore Sn concentrations ranging from 0 at.% to 20 at.% on waveguide-integrated PN and PIN heaters and observe a reduction in both the amorphization and crystallization energies in the 5--10 at.% range. At higher Sn content this trend reverses and the switching energy increases, which is suggestive of phase segregation when combined with TEM compositional analysis. A 10 at.% Sn device continues to switch over 1000 cycles, with observable degradation in the extinction ratio from 4.5 $\pm$ 0.3 dB to 2.4 $\pm$ 0.3 dB. Post-cycling imaging shows PCM migration and void formation which we believe can be further improved by enhanced encapsulation. Overall, Sn alloying offers a route to lower programming energy in integrated phase-change photonics without negatively affecting the switching speed relative to un-doped GST.

AI.tldr: Sn alloying of Ge2Sb2Te5 (5-10 at.%) reduces both amorphization and crystallization energies in waveguide-integrated phase-change photonics without changing device architecture or CMOS compatibility, though degradation and PCM migration occur over 1000 cycles.
AI.motivation: Integrated phase-change photonics enables non-volatile optical switching with zero static power draw, but the electrical energy required for reversible switching limits practical scaling. Prior efficiency improvements focused mainly on device optimization (microheater/waveguide redesign) rather than on the phase-change material itself.
AI.method: A materials-centered approach: alloying Sn into Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) without altering device structure or CMOS compatibility. Sn concentrations from 0 to 20 at.% were studied on waveguide-integrated PN and PIN heaters, combined with TEM compositional analysis.
AI.result: Both amorphization and crystallization energies decrease in the 5-10 at.% Sn range; at higher Sn content the trend reverses and switching energy increases, suggesting phase segregation (corroborated by TEM). A 10 at.% Sn device switched over 1000 cycles with extinction ratio degradation from 4.5 +/- 0.3 dB to 2.4 +/- 0.3 dB. Post-cycling imaging revealed PCM migration and void formation.
AI.conclusion: Sn alloying offers a route to lower programming energy in integrated phase-change photonics without negatively affecting switching speed relative to undoped GST. PCM migration and void formation may be mitigated by enhanced encapsulation.

title: Sign problem and criticality in world-line quantum Monte Carlo methods
summary: Discussions of the sign problem usually focus on its role as the primary limitation of the applicability of quantum Monte Carlo methods for reliably solving quantum many-body models. Its behavior as a function of spatial lattice size, doping, temperature, and interaction strengths has been carefully characterized within the determinant quantum Monte Carlo algorithm. Here, we consider the much less well-explored question of the temperature- and size-dependence of the sign problem in the world-line quantum Monte Carlo method. We review how, in this algorithm, even sampling the partition function of free fermions yields a sign problem, which we connect to non-analytic behavior in the corresponding reference model, hard-core bosons on a lattice. The latter exhibits a finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transition in 2D, and we show how this non-analytic behavior is imprinted on the average sign of the weights for the corresponding free fermion 2D tight-binding model. Our results thus show how phase-transition information can remain encoded in the sign problem even after direct sign sampling becomes impractical.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the temperature- and size-dependence of the sign problem in world-line quantum Monte Carlo, showing that the average sign for free fermions encodes non-analytic behavior tied to a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the corresponding hard-core boson reference model.
AI.motivation: The sign problem is the primary obstacle to applying quantum Monte Carlo to quantum many-body models. While its behavior has been well characterized in determinant quantum Monte Carlo, its temperature- and size-dependence in world-line quantum Monte Carlo remains much less explored.
AI.method: The authors review how sampling the partition function of free fermions produces a sign problem in world-line quantum Monte Carlo, and connect this to non-analytic behavior in the reference hard-core boson lattice model. They analyze the imprint of the finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in 2D on the average sign of the weights for the corresponding free fermion 2D tight-binding model.
AI.result: Even sampling free fermions yields a sign problem in world-line quantum Monte Carlo. The non-analytic behavior of the hard-core boson reference model, which exhibits a finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in 2D, is imprinted on the average sign of the weights for the free fermion 2D tight-binding model.
AI.conclusion: Phase-transition information can remain encoded in the sign problem even after direct sign sampling becomes impractical.

title: Nuclear quantum effects enhance diffusion in supercooled ammonia through accelerated pyramidal inversion
summary: In liquid ammonia, an imbalance between available hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites limits water-like tetrahedral connectivity, leaving sparse and short-lived associations within a densely packed liquid. We ask whether quantum-sensitive local rearrangements can nevertheless contribute appreciably to diffusion in this weakly connected liquid. We compare classical and thermostatted ring polymer molecular dynamics from 170 to 250 K using an r$^2$SCAN-trained machine learning force field. Ammonia can change its molecular geometry as the nitrogen atom passes through the plane of the three hydrogen atoms, a motion known as pyramidal inversion. Nuclear quantum effects increase the inversion rate and reduce its apparent activation energy. Inversion events are accompanied by transient reductions in hydrogen-bond coordination and local density within the first solvation shell. Although nuclear quantum effects lower density and viscosity throughout the studied range, diffusion remains only weakly affected in the warmer liquid. The quantum enhancement of diffusion emerges below approximately 210 K and reaches 18% at 170 K, tracking the enhancement of cage escape. These observations support an inversion-assisted contribution to diffusion, in which a spatially localized, quantum-sensitive internal motion couples to cage relaxation without a persistent tetrahedral network.

AI.tldr: Nuclear quantum effects enhance pyramidal inversion in liquid ammonia, and this inversion-assisted cage relaxation contributes appreciably to diffusion only in the cold, weakly connected liquid below ~210 K.
AI.motivation: Liquid ammonia lacks the balanced hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor ratio needed for water-like tetrahedral connectivity, so its intermolecular associations are sparse and short-lived. The authors ask whether quantum-sensitive local rearrangements (pyramidal inversion) can nonetheless contribute appreciably to diffusion in this weakly connected liquid.
AI.method: Classical and thermostatted ring polymer molecular dynamics simulations from 170 to 250 K using an r2SCAN-trained machine learning force field, analyzing inversion rates, activation energies, hydrogen-bond coordination, local density, viscosity, and cage escape.
AI.result: Nuclear quantum effects increase the pyramidal inversion rate and reduce its apparent activation energy. Inversion events coincide with transient reductions in hydrogen-bond coordination and local density in the first solvation shell. Quantum effects lower density and viscosity across the range, but diffusion is weakly affected in warmer liquid; the quantum enhancement of diffusion emerges below ~210 K, reaching 18% at 170 K and tracking enhanced cage escape.
AI.conclusion: These findings support an inversion-assisted mechanism of diffusion, in which a spatially localized, quantum-sensitive internal motion couples to cage relaxation without requiring a persistent tetrahedral network.

title: On the Relation Between the Boson Peak and the Vibrational Phases in Glasses
summary: The boson peak is a vibrational feature commonly found in glassy and disordered systems described as the deviation from the scaling of the Debye model ($g({E}){\propto}{E}^2$). Despite much interest, the microscopic nature of the vibrations is only anecdotally discussed. Here we report how the boson peak appears in conjunction with a crossover from localized to extended but non-wave-like and coincide with a maximum in phase coherence and spatial periodicity. Our analyses provide new insights into the microscopic origin of the boson peak across a wide range of glasses.

AI.tldr: The boson peak in glasses arises at a crossover from localized to extended non-wave-like vibrations, coinciding with maximal phase coherence and spatial periodicity.
AI.motivation: The boson peak is a ubiquitous vibrational feature in glassy/disordered systems, defined as a deviation from Debye scaling (g(E) ∝ E²). Despite extensive interest, its microscopic vibrational nature has only been discussed anecdotally, leaving its origin unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze how the boson peak emerges in relation to the vibrational character, tracking the crossover from localized to extended non-wave-like vibrations and correlating it with measures of phase coherence and spatial periodicity.
AI.result: The boson peak appears together with a crossover from localized to extended but non-wave-like vibrations, and coincides with a maximum in phase coherence and spatial periodicity.
AI.conclusion: These analyses offer new microscopic insight into the origin of the boson peak, proposed to hold across a wide range of glasses.

title: Three-Dimensional Shankar Skyrmions in Frustrated Antiferromagnets
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures, and a supplemental material
summary: We formulate a continuum theory for three-dimensional (3D) Shankar skyrmions in frustrated chiral antiferromagnets (AFs) and derive the conditions for metastable finite-size $π_3(SO(3))$ solitons. A Derrick--Hobart scaling analysis shows that exchange, Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interaction (DMI), anisotropy, and frustration can balance to set a finite equilibrium size. We identify two microscopic routes to this common topological and stabilization framework: intrinsic rotation-frame order in noncollinear AFs and an $\mathbb{S}^3$ extension of an amplitude-softened Néel field. In the latter, the smooth four-component texture projects onto a Néel field containing a spatially separated pair of oppositely charged Bloch points. Numerical minimization yields metastable monopole textures, while the effective dynamics identifies coherent breathing oscillations as their characteristic finite-frequency collective mode. Our results provide a microscopic framework for the statics and dynamics of Shankar skyrmions and identify frustrated chiral AFs as promising hosts of 3D non-Abelian topological textures.

AI.tldr: A continuum theory is developed for 3D Shankar skyrmions in frustrated chiral antiferromagnets, showing that exchange, DMI, anisotropy, and frustration balance to stabilize finite-size π₃(SO(3)) solitons, with numerical solutions revealing metastable monopole textures and breathing-mode dynamics.
AI.motivation: Three-dimensional topological solitons classified by π₃(SO(3)), such as Shankar skyrmions, are of broad interest as non-Abelian topological textures, but a microscopic framework connecting them to realistic magnetic materials and identifying concrete hosting systems with a finite equilibrium size has been lacking.
AI.method: A continuum theory is formulated for 3D Shankar skyrmions in frustrated chiral antiferromagnets, with Derrick–Hobart scaling analysis used to establish size stabilization. Two microscopic routes are identified: intrinsic rotation-frame order in noncollinear AFs, and an S³ extension of an amplitude-softened Néel field whose four-component texture projects onto a Néel field with a spatially separated pair of oppositely charged Bloch points. Numerical minimization and effective dynamics are then applied.
AI.result: Derrick–Hobart scaling shows exchange, Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction, anisotropy, and frustration can balance to set a finite equilibrium size. Numerical minimization yields metastable monopole textures, and the effective dynamics identifies coherent breathing oscillations as the characteristic finite-frequency collective mode.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a microscopic framework for the statics and dynamics of Shankar skyrmions and identifies frustrated chiral antiferromagnets as promising hosts of 3D non-Abelian topological textures.

title: $β$-Oslo and Shape analyses with unresolved parent-state mixtures
summary: An unresolved mixture of beta-decaying ground and isomeric states populates a common daughter nucleus through different excitation-energy and spin-parity distributions. A framework is developed to determine when such data admit conventional $β$-Oslo and Shape analyses and which quantities remain identifiable. The physical primary-$γ$ distribution is an average of separately normalized branching kernels; the global parent fraction does not, in general, equal the fraction in an excitation-energy bin or an accepted primary-$γ$ sample. Population invariance, Oslo factorization, and recovery of the total nuclear level density are separated. An exact log-linear compatibility test and a lower-cascade replacement identity isolate factorization and first-generation-subtraction effects. For Shape analysis, matched final-state spins and parities remove common angular-momentum factors but can retain excitation-dependent E1/M1 weights. A graph representation gives consistency conditions and exposes the information lost when only one fixed final-state separation is measured. Deterministic spin-parity-resolved cascade benchmarks reproduce the population-invariant limit and exhibit both exact factorization with an effective, rather than total, level density and small matrix residuals accompanied by appreciable shape errors. Evaluated $\rb\rightarrow\sr$ properties specify a relevant application, including two $2^+$ candidate final states and time-dependent parent mixing. The numerical examples are controlled synthetic tests, not an extraction from $^{90}$Rb data. The results provide criteria for interpreting unresolved-parent measurements and for identifying the additional observations required for population-aware inference.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an identifiability framework for beta-Oslo and Shape analyses when an unresolved mixture of beta-decaying ground and isomeric parent states feeds a common daughter, specifying when conventional analyses remain valid and which quantities are recoverable.
AI.motivation: Unresolved mixtures of beta-decaying ground and isomeric states populate a common daughter nucleus via distinct excitation-energy and spin-parity distributions. Conventional beta-Oslo and Shape analyses implicitly assume a single parent, so it is unclear under what conditions such data are interpretable and which physical quantities remain identifiable.
AI.method: The primary-gamma distribution is modeled as an average of separately normalized branching kernels, distinguishing global parent fraction from the fraction in an excitation-energy bin or accepted primary-gamma sample. Population invariance, Oslo factorization, and total level-density recovery are treated separately. An exact log-linear compatibility test and a lower-cascade replacement identity isolate factorization and first-generation-subtraction effects. For Shape analysis, a graph representation yields consistency conditions, and deterministic spin-parity-resolved cascade benchmarks test the population-invariant limit.
AI.result: The global parent fraction generally differs from bin- or sample-resolved fractions. Matched final-state spins and parities in Shape analysis remove common angular-momentum factors but can retain excitation-dependent E1/M1 weights. Benchmarks reproduce the population-invariant limit and show exact factorization with an effective (not total) level density, plus small matrix residuals accompanied by appreciable shape errors. Evaluated Rb-to-Sr properties provide a relevant application with two 2+ candidate final states and time-dependent parent mixing.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides criteria for interpreting unresolved-parent measurements and identifies the additional observations needed for population-aware inference. Numerical examples are controlled synthetic tests, not an extraction from 90Rb data.

title: MyTm: An Automated Melting Temperature Calculation Toolkit
summary: Melting temperature calculation is one of the important topics in computational materials science. In high-throughput in silico screening and artificial intelligence assisted design of materials, it usually requires a rapid and autonomous assessment of the melting temperature of the target. Unfortunately, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the melting point require many cumbersome and manual operations, making large-scale calculation of the melting point challenging. In this work, we introduce MyTm, a toolkit that employs MD to automatically determine the melting point. The method is fully modularized, and by combining these modules, the program enables fully automated melting calculations by using commonly adopted approaches, including the direct-heating method, the void method, the modified void method, the solid-liquid coexistence method, and the Z method. Moreover, a machine learning (ML) method is proposed and employed to recognize and classify the solid like and liquid like atoms, which effectively resolve the low accuracy issue in conventional classification approaches, thus making the automated high throughput pipeline of melting-point calculation possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm have been demonstrated by several well studied systems.

AI.tldr: MyTm is a modular toolkit that fully automates molecular dynamics melting-point calculations and uses a machine learning classifier for solid-like/liquid-like atoms to enable high-throughput screening.
AI.motivation: Melting temperature calculation is a key topic in computational materials science, and high-throughput in silico screening and AI-assisted materials design require rapid, autonomous assessment of melting temperature. However, conventional MD melting-point simulations demand many cumbersome manual operations, making large-scale melting-point calculation challenging.
AI.method: The authors introduce MyTm, a fully modularized MD-based toolkit for automatic melting-point determination. By combining its modules, the program enables fully automated melting calculations using commonly adopted approaches: the direct-heating method, the void method, the modified void method, the solid-liquid coexistence method, and the Z method. In addition, a machine learning method is proposed and employed to recognize and classify solid-like and liquid-like atoms.
AI.result: The ML-based classification effectively resolves the low accuracy issue of conventional classification approaches, thereby making an automated high-throughput melting-point calculation pipeline possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm are demonstrated on several well-studied systems.
AI.conclusion: MyTm provides a modular, automated solution for MD melting-point calculation, with ML-based atom classification enabling accurate high-throughput screening, as validated on several well-studied systems.

title: Excursion-Resolved Thermodynamic Inference without Observing Reverse Transitions
summary: Experiments often detect only selected transitions, leaving the underlying state dynamics and dissipation hidden. We show that waiting-time distributions between directed visible events can reconstruct the boundary dynamics without observing the reverse of every detected transition. Under a simple source-target closure condition, they determine visible rates and the hidden excursions connecting observed states, yielding a rigorous lower bound on total entropy production that improves the standard waiting-time estimate when reverse events are available. Remarkably, observing only a spanning directed cycle is sufficient to identify the full Markov generator, even when all reverse cycle edges and other microscopic transitions remain unseen.

AI.tldr: Waiting-time distributions between directed visible events can reconstruct hidden boundary dynamics and, under a source-target closure condition, identify the full Markov generator from only a spanning directed cycle, yielding a tighter lower bound on total entropy production.
AI.motivation: Experiments often detect only selected transitions, leaving the underlying state dynamics and dissipation hidden, so a method is needed to reconstruct dynamics and bound entropy production without observing every reverse transition.
AI.method: The authors use waiting-time distributions between directed visible events. Under a source-target closure condition, these distributions determine visible rates and the hidden excursions connecting observed states, giving a rigorous lower bound on total entropy production. They further analyze the case where only a spanning directed cycle is observed.
AI.result: The waiting-time distributions reconstruct the boundary dynamics without observing the reverse of every detected transition; the derived entropy-production bound improves the standard waiting-time estimate when reverse events are available. Observing only a spanning directed cycle suffices to identify the full Markov generator, even when all reverse cycle edges and other microscopic transitions remain unseen.
AI.conclusion: Hidden dynamics can be rigorously inferred from directed visible event statistics, enabling tighter thermodynamic bounds and full generator identification from minimal observations.

title: Ab initio calculated diamagnetic and paramagnetic susceptibility of carbonate minerals
summary:
The anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) is a widely used tool to infer rock fabrics, yet quantitative interpretation is limited by sparse single-crystal magnetic properties for rock-forming minerals and by the difficulty of separating intrinsic diamagnetism from impurity-related magnetism. Here we use density-functional theory (DFT) combined with perturbation theory to compute the diamagnetic susceptibility and AMS of calcite-group carbonates (calcite, magnesite, and dolomite) and to quantify the additional paramagnetic contribution from transition-metal doping.
  For pure calcite, the calculated susceptibility and its anisotropy are in good agreement with published single-crystal measurements, validating the ab initio approach for diamagnetic phases. We provide improved intrinsic diamagnetic reference values for magnesite and dolomite, for which experimental susceptibilities are commonly affected by magnetic impurities. To address impurity effects explicitly, we model Fe and Mn substitution in calcite using supercells. The computed spin moments reproduce expected high-spin states (Fe$^{2+}$, $S=2$; Mn$^{2+}$, $S=5/2$) and yield a susceptibility anisotropy per Fe concentration that matches the experimental slope. The strong anisotropy is primarily governed by an orbital contribution tied to the crystallographic $c$-axis rather than by spin-orbit coupling, highlighting orbital magnetisation as a key but numerically challenging ingredient for modelling of paramagnetic AMS in carbonates.

AI.tldr: DFT plus perturbation theory quantifies diamagnetic susceptibility and AMS of calcite-group carbonates and isolates the paramagnetic AMS contribution from Fe/Mn doping.
AI.motivation: AMS is widely used to infer rock fabrics, but quantitative interpretation is hindered by scarce single-crystal magnetic data for rock-forming minerals and by the difficulty of separating intrinsic diamagnetism from impurity-related magnetism.
AI.method: Density-functional theory (DFT) combined with perturbation theory to compute diamagnetic susceptibility and AMS for calcite, magnesite, and dolomite; supercell models of Fe and Mn substitution in calcite to capture impurity effects.
AI.result: Calculated susceptibility and anisotropy of pure calcite agree with published single-crystal measurements; improved intrinsic diamagnetic reference values are provided for magnesite and dolomite; computed spin moments reproduce high-spin Fe2+ (S=2) and Mn2+ (S=5/2), and the susceptibility anisotropy per Fe concentration matches the experimental slope. The strong anisotropy is governed mainly by an orbital contribution tied to the crystallographic c-axis rather than by spin-orbit coupling.
AI.conclusion: Ab initio methods validate diamagnetic AMS in carbonates and provide impurity-corrected references; orbital magnetisation is a key but numerically challenging ingredient for modelling paramagnetic AMS in carbonates.

title: Quantum quenches of scar states in the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki model via Clifford augmented tensor network simulation
summary: Clifford augmented methods have emerged as a powerful technique to simulate quantum circuits and many-body systems by exploiting the stabiliser structure found in said systems, whilst additionally enabling one to readily quantify the non-stabilizerness (i.e.\ magic) present. In this work, we utilise a qudit Clifford augmented simulation method to probe the presence of magic in the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) model, finding that its ground state and scar states are highly magical as quantified by their Stabiliser Rényi Entropy (SRE).
