Nevertheless, owing to its low entanglement structure, these states are still readily expressible as a Clifford augmented Matrix Product State with low bond-dimension and moreover may be time-evolved using the Clifford augmented time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) algorithm. We utilise Clifford augmented TDVP to study the string order dynamics in the scar states of the AKLT model after a quench within the Haldane phase to the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian. We observe that there is a decay of string order following the quench, which is more pronounced with increasing bimagnon number. This finding highlights the sensitivity of string order in the AKLT scar states to symmetry-preserving quenches, even when the initial and final Hamiltonians belong to the same topological phase.

AI.tldr: The AKLT ground and scar states are highly magical (per Stabiliser Rényi Entropy) yet remain efficiently representable as low-bond-dimension Clifford-augmented MPS, enabling Clifford-augmented TDVP simulations of string-order dynamics after a quench.
AI.motivation: Clifford-augmented methods can simulate quantum circuits and many-body systems while quantifying non-stabilizerness (magic). The authors aim to probe magic in the AKLT model and use the method to study quench dynamics of its scar states.
AI.method: A qudit Clifford-augmented simulation method is applied to the AKLT model, quantifying magic via Stabiliser Rényi Entropy. States are expressed as Clifford-augmented Matrix Product States (low bond dimension), and Clifford-augmented time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) is used to evolve scar states after a quench within the Haldane phase to the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The AKLT ground state and scar states are found to be highly magical as measured by SRE. Despite this, their low entanglement allows efficient Clifford-augmented MPS representation. String order decays after the quench, with the decay becoming more pronounced as bimagnon number increases.
AI.conclusion: String order in AKLT scar states is sensitive to symmetry-preserving quenches even when initial and final Hamiltonians lie in the same topological phase, underscoring the utility of Clifford-augmented methods for probing magic and dynamics in many-body systems.

title: A Visual Understanding of Circular Dichroism Spectroscopy: The Case of Interacting Chromophores
summary: Exciton coupling shapes the photophysical and chiroptical properties of molecular aggregates, but a microscopic, real-space understanding of how intermolecular interactions generate circular dichroism (CD) remains incomplete. Here, we computationally investigate the microscopic origins of CD in coupled molecular dimers to separate intermolecular (topological) from intramolecular (intrinsic) chirality. A combination of time-dependent density functional theory and transition chiral tensor (TCT) analysis provides a quantitative, visually intuitive framework showing how electronic coupling strength, intermolecular separation, and relative angular orientation govern chiroptical response. We find that pairs of individually achiral chromophores exhibit robust, topological chiroptical signals which give rise to the conventional Cotton effect, a standard interpretation of derivative features in circular dichroism spectra. We next establish that intrinsically chiral chromophores, on the other hand, disrupt the Cotton effect due to the competition between intrinsic chirality and topological chirality. This work establishes a foundation for interpreting exciton-coupled CD spectra in molecular aggregates, supramolecular assemblies, and nanostructures using the TCT approach, which offers an attractive tool for analyzing chiroptical responses in complex multi-chromophore systems relevant to emerging quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This work computationally separates topological (intermolecular) from intrinsic (intramolecular) chirality in coupled molecular dimers using TDDFT and transition chiral tensor (TCT) analysis, showing that achiral chromophore pairs give robust Cotton effects while intrinsically chiral chromophores disrupt them via competing chirality.
AI.motivation: Exciton coupling governs the photophysical and chiroptical properties of molecular aggregates, yet a microscopic, real-space understanding of how intermolecular interactions generate circular dichroism (CD) remains incomplete.
AI.method: The authors perform computational investigation of the microscopic origins of CD in coupled molecular dimers, combining time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) with transition chiral tensor (TCT) analysis to separate intermolecular (topological) from intramolecular (intrinsic) chirality.
AI.result: Pairs of individually achiral chromophores exhibit robust topological chiroptical signals producing the conventional Cotton effect; intrinsically chiral chromophores disrupt the Cotton effect due to competition between intrinsic and topological chirality. Electronic coupling strength, intermolecular separation, and relative angular orientation govern the chiroptical response.
AI.conclusion: The TCT approach establishes a foundation for interpreting exciton-coupled CD spectra in molecular aggregates, supramolecular assemblies, and nanostructures, offering an attractive tool for analyzing chiroptical responses in complex multi-chromophore systems relevant to emerging quantum technologies.

title: Eigenstate thermalization at the edge of the many-body spectrum
summary: It is well-known that thermalization breaks down in presence of an extensive number of symmetries or conservation laws that are mutually compatible or commuting with each other. We ask here how an extensive number of mutually incompatible local symmetries govern eigenstate thermalization (ETH). We will investigate this through models within the class of bond-dependent $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric quantum spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ Hamiltonians that naturally admit this structure. This leads to exponentially large degeneracies in the spectrum governed by the incompatible symmetry structure. Here, using spectral diagnostics, we show that non-integrability can survive despite extensively many conserved quantities when they are incompatible. Furthermore, we show that ETH behavior persists deep into the many-body spectral edge due to this structure. In other words, incompatible local symmetries enable a mechanism to obtain enough thermodynamic entropy at low excitation energy densities to make ETH operational or predictive near the ground state.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how extensively many mutually incompatible local symmetries affect eigenstate thermalization (ETH) in bond-dependent Z2-symmetric spin-1/2 Hamiltonians. Despite exponentially large degeneracies from the incompatible symmetry structure, the authors show that non-integrability survives and ETH persists deep into the many-body spectral edge, enabling ETH to remain predictive near the ground state.
AI.motivation: It is well-established that thermalization and ETH break down when there are extensively many commuting (mutually compatible) conservation laws or symmetries. However, the effect of an extensive number of mutually incompatible local symmetries on ETH is unexplored, motivating this investigation.
AI.method: The authors study models within the class of bond-dependent Z2-symmetric quantum spin-1/2 Hamiltonians, which naturally harbor an extensive number of mutually incompatible local symmetries. They employ spectral diagnostics to assess non-integrability and ETH behavior.
AI.result: The incompatible symmetry structure produces exponentially large degeneracies in the spectrum. Spectral diagnostics reveal that non-integrability can survive despite extensively many conserved quantities when these are incompatible. Moreover, ETH behavior persists deep into the many-body spectral edge.
AI.conclusion: Incompatible local symmetries provide a mechanism to obtain sufficient thermodynamic entropy at low excitation energy densities, making ETH operational and predictive near the ground state—contrary to the usual breakdown of thermalization with extensive commuting symmetries.

title: Nonrelativistic expansions of Dirac-Coulomb energy and first order relativistic Breit potential corrections for light Atomic and molecular systems
summary: The nonrelativistic expansion method is applied to the Dirac-Coulomb energy and first order relativistic Breit potential corrections for light atomic and molecular systems to derive high-order effective energy correction operators for few-body systems. It is found that effective operators at the $mα^8$ order contain incompletely separable divergences. These divergences must be canceled jointly with divergences arising from second- and third-order perturbations of lower-order energy correction operators, and such cancellation can be accomplished automatically by the nonrelativistic numerical expansion approach. Using Gaussian basis sets, we numerically compute contributions to the Dirac-Coulomb energy and relativistic Breit potential corrections up to order $mα^8$ for the ground states of the hydrogen atom, hydrogen molecular ion, helium atom, and hydrogen molecule. These results confirm the reliability of the present method and enable its extension to more complex systems.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the nonrelativistic expansion method to derive high-order effective energy correction operators (up to $m\alpha^8$) for light few-body atomic and molecular systems, resolving divergence cancellation and numerically computing corrections for H, H$_2^+$, He, and H$_2$.
AI.motivation: High-precision energy corrections beyond leading relativistic orders are needed for light atomic and molecular systems. At the $m\alpha^8$ order, effective operators develop incompletely separable divergences that require careful treatment with contributions from higher-order perturbations of lower-order operators.
AI.method: The nonrelativistic expansion method is applied to Dirac-Coulomb energy and first-order relativistic Breit potential corrections to derive effective energy correction operators. Incomplete divergences at $m\alpha^8$ are shown to cancel jointly with those from second- and third-order perturbations of lower-order operators, handled automatically via the nonrelativistic numerical expansion. Gaussian basis sets are used for numerical evaluation.
AI.result: Contributions to Dirac-Coulomb energy and relativistic Breit corrections up to $m\alpha^8$ are numerically computed for ground states of the hydrogen atom, hydrogen molecular ion, helium atom, and hydrogen molecule, confirming the reliability of the method.
AI.conclusion: The method reliably yields high-order relativistic energy corrections and can be extended to more complex few-body systems.

title: Light-driven Modulation of 1-bit Metamaterial Unit Cells and Arrays
summary: Shape-morphing materials have the potential to realise simple, tunable telecommunication arrays without the need for complex circuitry. However, existing devices either lack individual cell control, or require an integrated power supply, reducing their beamsteering ability and increasing size, weight and power consumption. This paper presents a simple, photothermally activated 1-bit reflectarray unit cell requiring no integrated power sources. The unit cell consists of dimer elements, which are connected or disconnected via a photothermally activated electrical bridge to achieve modulation. The paper discusses the shape memory materials used for switching, and presents a design for a photothermal switching mechanism. The unit cell is validated by waveguide experiments, showing strong agreement with simulations at the working frequency of 3.7GHz. Finally, a 4-cell array is created. Each cell is activated sequentially, with good agreement between simulation and experiment, demonstrating the ability to control each cell exclusively. This study therefore demonstrates that a 1-bit unit cell can be photothermally configured without complicated electronics or an integrated power supply, opening the door to a new class of shape-morphing reflectarray.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a photothermally activated 1-bit reflectarray unit cell using shape-memory-material dimer elements bridged by a photothermal electrical switch, requiring no integrated power supply. A 4-cell array with sequential activation demonstrates exclusive per-cell control, validated by waveguide experiments at 3.7 GHz.
AI.motivation: Shape-morphing materials could enable simple, tunable telecommunication arrays without complex circuitry, but existing devices either lack individual cell control or need an integrated power supply, which limits beamsteering and increases size, weight, and power consumption.
AI.method: The authors design a 1-bit reflectarray unit cell composed of dimer elements connected or disconnected by a photothermally activated electrical bridge. They select shape memory materials for switching, design a photothermal switching mechanism, fabricate the unit cell, and validate it via waveguide experiments against simulations at 3.7 GHz, then build and test a 4-cell array with sequential activation.
AI.result: Waveguide experiments on the unit cell show strong agreement with simulations at 3.7 GHz. The 4-cell array, activated cell-by-cell, also matches simulation well, demonstrating exclusive control of each cell.
AI.conclusion: A 1-bit unit cell can be photothermally configured without complicated electronics or an integrated power supply, opening the door to a new class of shape-morphing reflectarrays.

title: Optical observation of interlayer spin correlation
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures (main text), 7 supplementary figures, 1 supplementary table. Includes Supplementary Information
summary: Spin correlations govern numerous collective behaviors of quantum materials, underpinning exotic phenomena such as unconventional superconductivity and topological magnetism. In layered materials, the interlayer spin correlation is important because it characterizes the magnetic ground state and determines spin transport across the interface. Yet interlayer spin correlations have remained hard to measure directly, leaving one of the most basic quantities of two-dimensional magnetism out of experimental reach. Here we provide the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations, using two-magnon Raman scattering in the van der Waals antiferromagnet (AFM) CrSBr, in remarkable agreement with a microscopic spin-wave model without any fitting parameter. Moreover, the two-magnon channel switches on only in the AFM state and vanishes when a magnetic field takes the crystal to a ferromagnetic state. We furthermore establish an exciton-mediated variant of the technique, where tuning the laser near the exciton resonance enhances the signal roughly tenfold due to the exciton's large oscillator strength. Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy thus opens a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, extendable to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates the first direct optical probe of interlayer spin correlations in a van der Waals antiferromagnet, using two-magnon Raman scattering in CrSBr, validated by a parameter-free spin-wave model and shown to be switchable by magnetic field and enhanced via exciton resonance.
AI.motivation: Interlayer spin correlations in layered materials are critical for defining the magnetic ground state and governing interfacial spin transport, yet they have remained experimentally inaccessible, leaving a fundamental quantity of two-dimensional magnetism unmeasured.
AI.method: Two-magnon Raman scattering is applied to the van der Waals antiferromagnet CrSBr, interpreted with a microscopic spin-wave model that requires no fitting parameter. An exciton-mediated variant is developed by tuning the laser near the exciton resonance.
AI.result: The two-magnon signal agrees remarkably well with the parameter-free spin-wave model, appears only in the AFM state, and disappears when a magnetic field drives the crystal into a ferromagnetic state. Near-exciton laser tuning enhances the signal roughly tenfold owing to the exciton's large oscillator strength.
AI.conclusion: Magnon-pair Raman spectroscopy provides a direct optical window into interlayer spin correlations in van der Waals magnets, with extendability to twisted bilayers and proximity-coupled heterostructures.

title: Logarithmic Quasi-Long-Range Order and Novel Continuous Phase Transition in the Two-Dimensional $XY$ Model with $1/r^4$ Interaction
summary: We investigate the phase diagram and critical properties of the two-dimensional classical XY model with interactions decaying as $1/r^{2+σ}$. At the marginal case $σ=2$, we show that the low-temperature phase is characterized by logarithmic quasi-long-range order (log-QLRO), where spin correlations decay as a power of the logarithm of distance, $C(r)\sim(\ln r)^{-η_\ell}$ with $η_\ell\propto T$, and that the transition into this phase is a continuous transition beyond both the Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson paradigm and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless mechanism. Our analysis combines a near-exact Gaussian spin-wave theory, an adiabatic renormalization-group analysis, and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations. We find that the $1/r^4$ interaction logarithmically modifies the spin-wave stiffness kernel as $γ(k)\simeqκk^2\ln(1/k)$, which suppresses vortex proliferation and gives rise to a nonuniversal correlation-length exponent $ν\propto1/\sqrt{2πκ}$. Crucially, our simulations reveal that the short-range algebraic QLRO phase is unstable against a weak long-range perturbation for $σ\le2$. These results establish $σ=2$ as the crossover boundary between the long-range and short-range universality classes and provide a critical evaluation of recent theoretical proposals.

AI.tldr: At the marginal case σ=2 of the 2D classical XY model with 1/r^{2+σ} interactions, the low-temperature phase exhibits logarithmic quasi-long-range order with correlations decaying as (ln r)^{-η_ℓ}, and the transition is continuous, falling outside both Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson and Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless paradigms. σ=2 is established as the crossover boundary between long-range and short-range universality classes.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to resolve the nature of the phase diagram and critical properties of the 2D classical XY model with algebraically decaying interactions 1/r^{2+σ}, particularly at the marginal case σ=2, where standard paradigms (Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson and Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless) are expected to break down. It also seeks to critically evaluate recent theoretical proposals and determine whether the short-range algebraic QLRO phase survives weak long-range perturbations.
AI.method: The analysis combines three approaches: near-exact Gaussian spin-wave theory, an adiabatic renormalization-group analysis, and large-scale Monte Carlo simulations. The 1/r^4 interaction is shown to logarithmically modify the spin-wave stiffness kernel as γ(k) ≃ κk² ln(1/k).
AI.result: At σ=2, the low-temperature phase is a logarithmic quasi-long-range order (log-QLRO) state with C(r) ∼ (ln r)^{-η_ℓ} and η_ℓ ∝ T. The transition into this phase is continuous but beyond both Ginzburg-Landau-Wilson and BKT mechanisms. The logarithmically modified stiffness kernel suppresses vortex proliferation and yields a nonuniversal correlation-length exponent ν ∝ 1/√(2πκ). Simulations show that the short-range algebraic QLRO phase is unstable against a weak long-range perturbation for σ ≤ 2.
AI.conclusion: σ=2 is established as the crossover boundary between the long-range and short-range universality classes for the 2D classical XY model with 1/r^{2+σ} interactions. The marginal case exhibits a distinct log-QLRO phase and a non-BKT continuous transition, providing a critical evaluation of recent theoretical proposals.

title: Stress-based structure optimization for a range-separated hybrid van der Waals density functional
summary: Complex matter, often partly soft and pliable, is the generic form of material systems. We must therefore generally call on density functional theory (DFT) to first predict the atomic structure before we can use it to also characterize (expected) properties. A recent range-separated hybrid (RSH) van Waals density functional (vdW-DF), `vdW-DF2-ahbr' (abbreviated AHBR) [PRX 12, 041003 (2022)], shows promise as a high-accuracy predictor of both binding energies and structure, from molecules to solids. However, the present implementation in Quantum Espresso (QE) does not, in our experience, support robust stress-based unit-cell optimization of RSHs. Here we document and illustrate work enabling practical AHBR-based complex-matter discovery: We port the AHBR XC functional to the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) where use of stress-based DFT optimization is already stable also for RSHs. We test the implementation by comparing high-accuracy AHBR-QE and AHBR-VASP predictions of non-covalent molecular interactions and for structure and cohesion of simple bulk structures. We also illustrate and test the use of the new AHBR-VASP implementation to predict and understand (atomic and anti-ferromagnetic) structure in distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides. Finally, we illustrate use for complex-soft-matter discovery by predicting motifs for layer stacking in the C2N covalent-organic framework (COF) system [Nat. Commun. 6, 6486 (2015)].

AI.tldr: The AHBR range-separated hybrid van der Waals density functional is ported from Quantum Espresso to VASP to enable stable stress-based unit-cell optimization, validated against molecular interactions and bulk cohesion, and applied to distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides and C2N COF layer stacking.
AI.motivation: Complex matter is often partly soft and pliable, requiring DFT to first predict atomic structure before characterizing properties. The AHBR RSH vdW-DF shows promise as a high-accuracy predictor of binding energies and structure from molecules to solids, but its Quantum Espresso implementation does not robustly support stress-based unit-cell optimization of RSHs.
AI.method: The authors port the AHBR exchange-correlation functional to the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP), where stress-based DFT optimization is already stable for RSHs. They test the implementation by comparing high-accuracy AHBR-QE and AHBR-VASP predictions of non-covalent molecular interactions and of structure and cohesion in simple bulk structures. They further apply it to distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides and to C2N covalent-organic framework layer stacking motifs.
AI.result: The AHBR-VASP implementation yields predictions consistent with AHBR-QE for non-covalent molecular interactions and simple bulk structure and cohesion, while enabling robust stress-based unit-cell optimization. It also predicts and rationalizes atomic and anti-ferromagnetic structure in distorted-rocksalt metal monoxides and identifies layer-stacking motifs in the C2N COF system.
AI.conclusion: Porting AHBR to VASP enables practical, robust AHBR-based complex-matter discovery, including soft-matter and framework systems, by combining high-accuracy prediction of binding energies and structure with stable stress-based cell optimization.

title: Chiral quantum chaos around exponentially many zero modes in the quantum breakdown model
summary: The quantum breakdown model is a model of randomly interacting fermions, motivated by the physics of dielectric breakdown. Here, we establish classification of symmetry and quantum chaos in a zero-dimensional, all-to-all-interacting version of the quantum breakdown model. It exhibits the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ periodicity with respect to the number of fermionic modes, reminiscent of the symmetry classification of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model. A unique feature of the quantum breakdown model is that it realizes all the five classes with chiral symmetry and hosts an exponentially large number of many-body zero modes protected by the chiral index. We elucidate the separation and scaling of the spectral gap and demonstrate the symmetry-enriched hard-edge spectral statistics as signatures of quantum chaos in the chiral symmetry classes.

AI.tldr: This work classifies symmetries and quantum chaos in a zero-dimensional, all-to-all-interacting quantum breakdown model, revealing Z4 periodicity, realization of all five chiral symmetry classes, exponentially many many-body zero modes, and chiral hard-edge spectral statistics as quantum chaos signatures.
AI.motivation: The quantum breakdown model, motivated by dielectric breakdown physics, describes randomly interacting fermions, but a systematic understanding of its symmetry classification and quantum chaotic behavior—particularly in an all-to-all-interacting regime—has been lacking.
AI.method: The authors analyze a zero-dimensional, all-to-all-interacting version of the quantum breakdown model, performing symmetry classification analogous to that of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and examining spectral statistics, including the spectral gap and hard-edge behavior.
AI.result: The model exhibits Z4 periodicity with respect to the number of fermionic modes, reminiscent of SYK symmetry classification. It realizes all five classes with chiral symmetry and hosts an exponentially large number of many-body zero modes protected by the chiral index. The authors elucidate the separation and scaling of the spectral gap and identify symmetry-enriched hard-edge spectral statistics as signatures of quantum chaos.
AI.conclusion: The all-to-all-interacting quantum breakdown model provides a distinct platform for studying symmetry-enriched quantum chaos, characterized by Z4 periodicity, chiral symmetry classes, abundant protected zero modes, and hard-edge spectral statistics.

title: Spin Birefringence and Spin Polarized Transmission across p-wave Altermagnetic Heterostructure
summary: This paper investigates electron transport properties across N/AM interface or N/AM/N heterojunction. Based on Hamiltonians in the three regions, general wave functions are proposed and combined linear equations are constructed. Reflection and transmission coefficients as well as spin polarizatioin of the altermagnet heterostructure are obtained. When electron incident from normal metal to altermagnet, it is scattered and split into + branch and _ branch transmitting into altermagnet zone with separate refractive angles. Total internal reflection might happen to + branch. Critical angle of total reflection is determined by incident conditions and properties of AM material. In the heterostructure case, spin-up and spin-down electrons transmitted with same propagation directions but different transmission probabilities. Transmission and polarization periodically change with length of the junction. Exchange field and spin-splitting strength have pronounced effect on spin-polarized transmittance while the effect of spin-orbit coupling is quite small. Optimized system can be found by tuning parameters of the AM material. This study will lay the theoretical groundwork for experimental research on spin-selective outputs and spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: This theoretical study models electron transport across N/AM and N/AM/N altermagnet heterostructures using a Hamiltonian-based wave-function and linear-equation approach, revealing branch splitting, total internal reflection, and tunable spin-polarized transmission.
AI.motivation: Altermagnets are promising for spintronics because of their spin-split band structure, but their interfacial electron transport behavior needs a theoretical foundation. This paper aims to establish such groundwork for spin-selective outputs and spintronic device design.
AI.method: The authors define Hamiltonians for the normal metal (N) and altermagnet (AM) regions, propose general wave functions in each region, and construct combined linear equations. Solving these yields reflection and transmission coefficients and the spin polarization of N/AM and N/AM/N heterostructures.
AI.result: Electrons incident from N into AM split into + and − branches transmitting at separate refraction angles, with the + branch capable of total internal reflection at a critical angle set by incident conditions and AM properties. In the heterostructure, spin-up and spin-down electrons transmit along the same propagation direction but with different probabilities. Transmission and polarization oscillate periodically with junction length. Exchange field and spin-splitting strength strongly affect spin-polarized transmittance, whereas spin-orbit coupling has a minor effect.
AI.conclusion: The results show that the system can be optimized by tuning AM material parameters, providing theoretical groundwork for experimental studies on spin-selective outputs and spintronic devices.

title: Computing electron overlap integrals for Gausslet orbitals on cubic lattices
summary: Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice, introduced in [Steven R. White, J. Chem. Phys. 147, 244102 (2017)], represent a localized, smooth, and systematically refineable basis set featuring a "diagonal" approximability of the electron repulsion integral tensor. The present work develops efficient algorithms for evaluating overlap integrals required for electronic-structure simulations using these Gausslets, specifically the kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion integrals (both with and without the diagonal approximation). Computational efficiency improvements rest on the exploitation of translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries, a reordering and precomputation of nested sums, as well as an early truncation of small coefficients. Our algorithms reduce the number of electron repulsion integrals on a $5 \times 5 \times 5$ grid from $125^4 = 244140625$ to $324275$ due to symmetries, and achieve a wall-clock runtime for evaluating the remaining integrals with a truncation tolerance of $10^{-5}$ in under 2 seconds on a laptop computer. We apply the developed methodology to compute the ground state of the hydrogen atom and molecule as a demonstration.

AI.tldr: This work develops efficient algorithms for evaluating kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion integrals over Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice, exploiting translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries plus sum reordering, precomputation, and early truncation, reducing ERIs on a 5×5×5 grid from 244,140,625 to 324,275 and computing them in under 2 seconds on a laptop, demonstrated on the hydrogen atom and molecule.
AI.motivation: Gausslet orbitals provide a localized, smooth, systematically refineable basis with "diagonal" approximability of the electron repulsion integral tensor, but practical electronic-structure simulations require efficient evaluation of the underlying overlap integrals (kinetic, nuclear, electron repulsion, with and without the diagonal approximation). The paper addresses this need for fast integral evaluation.
AI.method: Algorithms exploit translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries; a reordering and precomputation of nested sums; and early truncation of small coefficients. Both the full and diagonally approximated electron repulsion integrals are treated.
AI.result: On a 5×5×5 grid, symmetries reduce the electron repulsion integrals from 125^4 = 244,140,625 to 324,275, and the remaining integrals with a truncation tolerance of 10^-5 are evaluated in under 2 seconds of wall-clock time on a laptop computer.
AI.conclusion: The developed methodology is applied to compute the ground state of the hydrogen atom and molecule as a demonstration, confirming the practical viability of the Gausslet integral algorithms.

title: Phase Separation in Fractonic Fluids: Coarsening, Interfaces, Nucleation, and Hyperuniformity in and out of Equilibrium
summary: We develop a theory of phase separation in fluids conserving higher-order multipole moments of a scalar density, and investigate the resulting coarsening dynamics, nucleation, and interfacial fluctuations. We find that higher-order conservation laws slow the relaxation of all phenomena investigated, whereas nonequilibrium violations of the fluctuation--dissipation theorem suppress density and interfacial fluctuations while hindering nucleation. Simulations support these predictions.

AI.tldr: A theory of phase separation under conserved higher-order multipole moments of a scalar density is developed, showing that higher-order conservation laws slow relaxation across coarsening, nucleation, and interfacial fluctuations, while non-equilibrium violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem suppresses fluctuations and hinders nucleation, with simulation confirmation.
AI.motivation: Conventional phase separation theory assumes conservation of a scalar density (zeroth moment). Many physical systems, however, conserve higher-order multipole moments, so the dynamics of phase separation under such constraints remain poorly understood.
AI.method: A continuum field theory is constructed for fluids in which higher-order multipole moments of a scalar density are conserved, and the coarsening dynamics, nucleation kinetics, and interfacial fluctuation spectrum are analyzed, supported by numerical simulations.
AI.result: Higher-order conservation laws generically slow the relaxation of all investigated phenomena. Non-equilibrium violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem suppresses both density and interfacial fluctuations and impedes nucleation. Simulations corroborate these analytical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Conservation of higher-order multipole moments and violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem qualitatively and quantitatively reshape phase separation kinetics, offering a framework for describing phase ordering in systems with multipole-conserving dynamics.

title: Results of Classical and Nonclassical theories of nucleation for ordering transition in barium titanate
summary: Results of classical and nonclassical approach to nucleation at the ordering phase transition in barium titanate are presented. A nonclassical nucleation model is applied to the first-order paraelectric cubic phase to ferroelectric tetragonal phase transition in barium titanate is considered.

AI.tldr: The paper compares classical and nonclassical nucleation approaches for the ordering (first-order paraelectric cubic → ferroelectric tetragonal) phase transition in barium titanate, applying a nonclassical nucleation model to this transition.
AI.motivation: Classical nucleation theory is widely used but often inadequate for describing ordering phase transitions, motivating the use of a nonclassical nucleation model to better capture the nucleation behavior at the paraelectric-to-ferroelectric transition in barium titanate.
AI.method: Both classical nucleation theory and a nonclassical nucleation model are applied to the first-order paraelectric cubic → ferroelectric tetragonal phase transition in barium titanate (BaTiO3).
AI.result: Results of the classical and nonclassical nucleation approaches are presented for the ordering phase transition in barium titanate.
AI.conclusion: The nonclassical nucleation model is relevant to describing the first-order paraelectric cubic to ferroelectric tetragonal transition in barium titanate, offering an alternative to the classical approach.

title: Tunability of the structural and magnetic transition in kagome material: PrIr$_3$B$_2$
summary: We report the temperature and pressure tunability of an unusual structural transformation associated with a two-step metal-insulator-metal (MIM) transition in the kagome lattice compound PrIr$_3$B$_2$ using synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction. At ambient conditions of temperature and pressure, the monoclinic ($C2/m$) and the hexagonal ($P6/mmm$) phases coexist as twinned structure in the crystal. As the temperature (pressure) is decreased (increased), PrIr$_3$B$_2$ converts fully to monoclinic structure at $T =$ 280 K (at ambient pressure) and $P =$ 1.2 GPa (at room temperature). Temperature dependence of the monoclinic structure at ambient pressure presents complex evolution of lattice parameters with weak but clearly discernable anomalies at \SI{\sim 250} {\K} and \SI{\sim 110} {\K}, which are correlated with the second MIM transition and the linear to nonlinear temperature-dependent resistivity crossover, respectively. These anomalies are likely due to some charge order state causing a partially gapped Fermi surface. The magnetic phase diagram of PrIr$_3$B$_2$ is also investigated from anisotropic measurements. At 10 K, a superzone gap opens near the antiferromagnetic transition, which does not close even in the polarized state. From the tunability of the crystal structure and magnetic and electronic ground state, promising electronic orders are indicated in this kagome metallic magnet.

AI.tldr: Synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows that the kagome compound PrIr3B2 undergoes a two-step metal-insulator-metal transition tied to a tunable monoclinic-hexagonal structural transformation, with coexisting phases at ambient conditions and weak lattice anomalies near 250 K and 110 K linked to charge order and a resistivity crossover.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand the coupling between crystal structure, magnetism, and electronic transport in the kagome metallic magnet PrIr3B2, particularly the origin of its unusual two-step metal-insulator-metal (MIM) transition and the role of temperature and pressure in tuning its structural ground state.
AI.method: Synchrotron X-ray powder diffraction was used to track the structural transformation under varying temperature and pressure. Temperature-dependent lattice parameters were measured at ambient pressure, and anisotropic magnetic measurements were performed to construct the magnetic phase diagram. The resistivity behavior was correlated with the structural and magnetic data.
AI.result: At ambient conditions, monoclinic (C2/m) and hexagonal (P6/mmm) phases coexist as a twinned structure. Cooling to 280 K or applying 1.2 GPa at room temperature drives a complete conversion to the monoclinic phase. Lattice parameters show weak anomalies near ~250 K and ~110 K, correlated with the second MIM transition and the linear-to-nonlinear resistivity crossover. A superzone gap opens near the antiferromagnetic transition at 10 K and persists even in the polarized state.
AI.conclusion: The tunable structural, magnetic, and electronic ground states of PrIr3B2 indicate promising electronic orders in this kagome metallic magnet, with a partially gapped Fermi surface likely arising from a charge order state.

title: Autocata: Reaction-network-guided autonomous catalyst screening via capability-centric AI
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the accessible space for catalyst discovery, yet executing complex screening campaigns still requires constant human intervention to bridge high-level reaction objectives with underlying computational pipelines. Here, we present Autocata, a knowledge-embedded autonomous agent that scales catalytic expertise by encoding multistep reaction pathways into reusable, language-invocable capabilities. Powered by a Transformer pretrained on two million catalyst-adsorbate structures, the system incorporates a capability registry of 79 adsorbate-specialized generative models spanning complex reaction networks across carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates. Given a high-level natural-language prompt, Autocata deconstructs reaction networks, queries and configures matching generative models, generates candidate surface configurations, enforces physical and geometric validity filtering, and coordinates machine-learning potentials evaluations to rank promising materials. Crucially, the agent adaptively reconfigures workflows when encountering capability boundaries or task bottlenecks. We demonstrate these capabilities across CH4 activation, nitrogen reduction reaction (N2RR), and CO2-to-methanol pathways. By shifting from static toolkits to an adaptive, language-driven computational infrastructure, Autocata lowers the barrier for expert-level catalyst discovery and offers a scalable paradigm for self-driving catalytic research.

AI.tldr: Autocata is a knowledge-embedded autonomous agent that encodes multistep reaction pathways into reusable, language-invocable capabilities, enabling end-to-end catalyst screening with minimal human intervention.
AI.motivation: AI has widened the accessible space for catalyst discovery, but running complex screening campaigns still demands constant human intervention to connect high-level reaction objectives with underlying computational pipelines.
AI.method: Autocata uses a Transformer pretrained on two million catalyst-adsorbate structures and a capability registry of 79 adsorbate-specialized generative models covering carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen intermediates. From a natural-language prompt, it deconstructs reaction networks, queries and configures matching generative models, generates candidate surface configurations, filters for physical and geometric validity, and coordinates machine-learning potential evaluations to rank materials, adaptively reconfiguring workflows at capability boundaries or bottlenecks.
AI.result: The agent is demonstrated across CH4 activation, nitrogen reduction reaction (N2RR), and CO2-to-methanol pathways.
AI.conclusion: By shifting from static toolkits to an adaptive, language-driven computational infrastructure, Autocata lowers the barrier to expert-level catalyst discovery and offers a scalable paradigm for self-driving catalytic research.

title: Designing Strongly Correlated Quantum Phases of Matter with Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States
summary: Designing a material with a desired property amounts to solving an inverse problem: finding the couplings of a microscopic Hamiltonian whose ground state exhibits that property. For strongly correlated quantum systems, solving this problem efficiently remains largely out of reach. To address this challenge, we present a general framework for ab initio inverse design based on Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States, a recent approach in which the ground states of a family of Hamiltonians are encoded in a single variational wave function. Because the ansatz depends explicitly on the couplings, any target property is a differentiable function of them, and the search for the right Hamiltonian reduces to gradient-based optimization in coupling space. We apply this approach to search for nonmagnetic phases of frustrated Heisenberg models on the square lattice with an increasing number of free next-nearest-neighbor couplings, aiming to identify new quantum spin liquid candidates. With a single coupling, the method recovers the known nonmagnetic window of the square $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model, whereas letting the two diagonal couplings vary independently reveals an extended nonmagnetic region connecting the square-lattice and anisotropic-triangular-lattice regimes. In a search space of eight independent couplings within a $2\times2$ unit cell, which contains several paradigmatic frustrated spin models, the optimization spontaneously converges to the $J_1$-$J_2$-$δ$ Heisenberg model, in which the diagonal couplings alternate between two values on neighboring plaquettes, a model recently proposed in the context of altermagnetism. Finite-size scaling up to $16\times16$ clusters in this optimal model shows that the ground state has no magnetic, dimer, or plaquette order, establishing it as a new quantum spin liquid candidate, distinct from those previously proposed on the square lattice.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a framework for ab initio inverse design of strongly correlated quantum materials using Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States, enabling gradient-based optimization in Hamiltonian coupling space to discover new quantum spin liquid candidates in frustrated Heisenberg models.
AI.motivation: Designing a material with a desired property is an inverse problem: finding microscopic Hamiltonian couplings whose ground state exhibits that property. For strongly correlated quantum systems, solving this efficiently remains largely out of reach.
AI.method: The approach is based on Foundation Neural-Network Quantum States, where ground states of a family of Hamiltonians are encoded in a single variational wave function that depends explicitly on the couplings. This makes any target property a differentiable function of the couplings, so finding the right Hamiltonian reduces to gradient-based optimization in coupling space. Applied to frustrated square-lattice Heisenberg models with increasing numbers of free next-nearest-neighbor couplings, up to eight independent couplings in a 2x2 unit cell.
AI.result: With a single coupling, the method recovers the known nonmagnetic window of the square J1-J2 Heisenberg model. Letting two diagonal couplings vary independently reveals an extended nonmagnetic region connecting square-lattice and anisotropic-triangular-lattice regimes. In a search space of eight couplings, optimization spontaneously converges to the J1-J2-delta Heisenberg model, with diagonal couplings alternating on neighboring plaquettes (a model recently proposed in altermagnetism context). Finite-size scaling up to 16x16 clusters shows no magnetic, dimer, or plaquette order.
AI.conclusion: The optimal model constitutes a new quantum spin liquid candidate on the square lattice, distinct from previously proposed ones.

title: Bilayer Lithium Niobate Acoustic Resonators for Spurious-Free Wideband Operation at 6 GHz
summary: The evolution of wireless communication standards toward higher frequencies and wider bandwidths places increasing demands on acoustic filter technologies. Conventional resonators face scaling limitations above 5 GHz, where lithographic constraints, reduced electromechanical coupling coefficient (k2eff), and spurious mode excitation hinder practical filter implementation. Here, we introduce a bilayer X-cut lithium niobate (LiNbO3) thickness-shear bulk acoustic resonator architecture that leverages symmetry engineering as a new design degree of freedom. By vertically stacking two piezoelectric thin films with a tailored bonding angle, the second-order thickness-shear mode (SH2, slow) is selectively excited. Furthermore, the fast thickness-shear modes inherent to X-cut LiNbO3 are suppressed, yielding a spurious-free in-band response. Devices operating around 6 GHz demonstrate a k2eff of approximately 35%, in close agreement with finite-element simulations and confirming the symmetry-driven mode selection mechanism. Proof-of-concept ladder filters demonstrate a fractional bandwidth of 18.6%, highlighting the wideband capabilities of the proposed architecture. The proposed configuration enables thickness-defined frequency scaling while maintaining high coupling and spectral purity, offering a promising platform for wideband radiofrequency filters in next-generation wireless systems.

AI.tldr: A bilayer X-cut LiNbO3 thickness-shear bulk acoustic resonator uses symmetry engineering (stacking two piezoelectric films at a tailored bonding angle) to selectively excite the slow SH2 mode and suppress fast shear spurious modes, achieving ~35% k2eff at ~6 GHz and 18.6% fractional bandwidth in a proof-of-concept ladder filter.
AI.motivation: Wireless standards are moving to higher frequencies and wider bandwidths, but conventional acoustic resonators struggle above 5 GHz due to lithographic scaling limits, reduced electromechanical coupling (k2eff), and spurious mode excitation, which impede practical filter implementation.
AI.method: The authors propose a bilayer X-cut lithium niobate (LiNbO3) thickness-shear bulk acoustic resonator architecture. Two piezoelectric thin films are vertically stacked with a tailored bonding angle, using symmetry engineering as a design degree of freedom to selectively excite the second-order thickness-shear mode (SH2, slow) while suppressing the fast thickness-shear modes intrinsic to X-cut LiNbO3.
AI.result: Devices around 6 GHz exhibit k2eff of approximately 35%, closely matching finite-element simulations and confirming the symmetry-driven mode selection mechanism. A proof-of-concept ladder filter achieves a fractional bandwidth of 18.6%, a spurious-free in-band response, and thickness-defined frequency scaling with high coupling and spectral purity.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry engineering in bilayer X-cut LiNbO3 resonators enables scalable, wideband, spurious-free acoustic filtering above 5 GHz, providing a promising platform for next-generation wireless RF filters.

title: Giant PhotoMagnetoDiode Effect
summary: We report the observation of a photomagnetodiode effect with a giant rectification ratio of 10 at a magnetic field of 0.1 T. The effect consists of a diode-like dependence of the photocurrent on the applied voltage that emerges in an external magnetic field. Such a pronounced nonreciprocity is observed in high-quality VPE-grown GaAs samples at low temperatures at interband photoexcitation. The photoconductivity is invariant upon reversing the polarity of both electric and magnetic fields. Similar behavior with even higher asymmetry ratio is observed in photoluminescence. The findings are well described by the theory of ambipolar drift of carriers in electric and magnetic fields together with fast surface recombination.

AI.tldr: A photomagnetodiode effect with a giant rectification ratio of 10 is observed in high-quality VPE-grown GaAs at low temperature under a magnetic field of 0.1 T, and is explained by ambipolar drift combined with fast surface recombination.
AI.motivation: To report and explain a pronounced nonreciprocal phenomenon—a magnetically induced diode-like photocurrent response—in semiconductors.
AI.method: Interband photoexcitation experiments on high-quality VPE-grown GaAs samples at low temperatures in an external magnetic field; measurement of photocurrent versus applied voltage, photoconductivity polarity dependence, and photoluminescence asymmetry; comparison with theory of ambipolar carrier drift in electric and magnetic fields including fast surface recombination.
AI.result: A giant rectification ratio of 10 is achieved at 0.1 T. The photocurrent shows diode-like voltage dependence emerging only in a magnetic field. Photoconductivity is invariant under reversal of both electric and magnetic field polarities. Photoluminescence exhibits even higher asymmetry. The findings agree well with the ambipolar drift and fast surface recombination theory.
AI.conclusion: The photomagnetodiode effect in GaAs is a genuine, magnetically controlled nonreciprocal phenomenon well described by ambipolar drift together with fast surface recombination, and it manifests similarly in photoluminescence.

title: Square-root growth of operator entanglement in an integrable brickwork circuit
comment: 4.5 pages and 17 pages of Supplemental Material
summary: It is widely expected that the von Neumann entanglement of a local operator grows at most logarithmically in integrable many-body systems in infinite volume. We give a counterexample in a four-state brickwork circuit whose gate is a permutation matrix solving the constant Yang--Baxter equation. The von Neumann operator entropy grows as $(\log2)\sqrt{t/π}+O(\log t)$, whereas fixed-index Rényi entropies grow linearly below index one and logarithmically above it. At fixed relative Hilbert--Schmidt error below one, matrix product operator simulations require a bond dimension growing at least as $\exp(c\sqrt t)$ for some $c>0$.

AI.tldr: A four-state brickwork circuit with a permutation-matrix gate solving the constant Yang–Baxter equation provides a counterexample to the expectation that von Neumann operator entanglement grows at most logarithmically in integrable systems: it grows as (log2)√(t/π)+O(log t).
AI.motivation: The widely held expectation is that von Neumann entanglement of a local operator grows at most logarithmically in integrable many-body systems in infinite volume. The paper aims to test this conjecture by constructing an integrable model that violates it.
AI.method: The authors construct a four-state brickwork quantum circuit whose two-site gate is a permutation matrix that solves the constant (i.e., parameter-independent) Yang–Baxter equation, then analyze the growth of operator entanglement entropies, distinguishing von Neumann entropy from fixed-index Rényi entropies, and assess matrix product operator simulability via required bond dimension.
AI.result: The von Neumann operator entropy grows as (log2)√(t/π)+O(log t), i.e., sublinearly but faster than logarithmically. Fixed-index Rényi entropies grow linearly below index one and logarithmically above index one. At fixed relative Hilbert–Schmidt error below one, matrix product operator simulations require bond dimension growing at least as exp(c√t) for some c>0.
AI.conclusion: Integrability does not universally cap von Neumann operator entanglement at logarithmic growth: an exactly solvable (Yang–Baxter) circuit exhibits √t growth, and this fast growth imposes super-polynomial bond dimension requirements on MPO simulation, with sharp index-dependent distinctions among Rényi entropies.

title: Single-particle detection of the Néel transition in LaCrO$_3$ microcrystals via widefield nitrogen-vacancy center magnetic imaging
summary: Rare-earth orthochromites exhibit rich, chemically tunable magnetic behavior, making them attractive for temperature sensing and temperature-dependent switching applications. Realizing this potential requires understanding how synthesis conditions and particle morphology influence the underlying Cr$^{3+}$ magnetic ordering. Orthochromite magnetism has traditionally been characterized by ensemble techniques such as neutron diffraction and SQUID magnetometry, which report only averaged magnetic properties and cannot access particle-level information. Here we use widefield nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry to image the stray magnetic fields of individual LaCrO$_3$ microcrystals produced via molten salt synthesis, resolving the antiferromagnetic Néel transition in single particles. Of the 18 particles measured between 278 and 298 K, five show a clear onset of magnetization near the ensemble Néel temperature, four show no measurable magnetic signal, and nine display temperature-independent signatures consistent with localized magnetic impurities undetected by ensemble measurements. Below the Néel temperature, particle magnetization remains fixed under a rotating in-plane field, consistent with canted antiferromagnetic ordering rather than paramagnetism, while repeated thermal cycling shows that the magnetic field pattern varies between cooldowns with certain features recurring at the same locations, consistent with micron-scale structurally pinned antiferromagnetic domains in which the sign of the weak ferromagnetic moment is set independently each time they pass through the Néel transition. These results establish single-particle NV magnetometry as a sensitive probe of magnetic ordering and domain structure in individual microcrystals, a key step toward correlating individual particle morphology and defect structure with magnetic ordering in orthochromites.

AI.tldr: Widefield NV magnetometry images stray fields of individual LaCrO3 microcrystals, resolving the antiferromagnetic Neel transition in single particles and revealing particle-to-particle heterogeneity and pinned antiferromagnetic domains.
AI.motivation: Rare-earth orthochromites have chemically tunable magnetism useful for temperature sensing and temperature-dependent switching, but exploiting this requires knowing how synthesis conditions and particle morphology affect Cr3+ magnetic ordering. Traditional ensemble methods (neutron diffraction, SQUID) only give averaged properties and cannot resolve particle-level behavior.
AI.method: Widefield nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry was used to image stray magnetic fields of individual LaCrO3 microcrystals made by molten salt synthesis, resolving the antiferromagnetic Neel transition in single particles. Measurements spanned 278-298 K on 18 particles, including rotating in-plane field tests and repeated thermal cycling.
AI.result: Of 18 particles, five showed clear magnetization onset near the ensemble Neel temperature, four showed no measurable magnetic signal, and nine displayed temperature-independent signatures consistent with localized magnetic impurities undetected by ensemble measurements. Below the Neel temperature magnetization stayed fixed under a rotating in-plane field, indicating canted antiferromagnetic ordering rather than paramagnetism. Repeated thermal cycling showed varying field patterns between cooldowns with some features recurring at the same locations.
AI.conclusion: Single-particle NV magnetometry is a sensitive probe of magnetic ordering and domain structure in individual microcrystals. Results are consistent with micron-scale structurally pinned antiferromagnetic domains whose weak ferromagnetic moment sign is set independently at each Neel transition, a key step toward correlating individual particle morphology and defect structure with magnetic ordering in orthochromites.

title: Multipartite entanglement hidden in vector-chiral correlations of spin-1/2 chains
summary: Characterizing entanglement in quantum materials through experimentally accessible observables remains a central challenge. Quantum Fisher information associated with sums of one-site spin operators provides one route by linking entanglement to measurable magnetic response functions. Extending this approach to local composite observables requires new entanglement bounds. Here we establish a rigorous bound for the total nearest-neighbour vector chirality of periodic spin-$1/2$ chains with an even number of sites. The quantum Fisher information per spin cannot exceed $k+1$ for any $k$-producible state, so exceeding this bound certifies entanglement depth of at least $k+1$. Combining infinite density-matrix renormalization group and thermal pure quantum-state calculations, we demonstrate multipartite entanglement encoded in vector-chiral correlations at zero and finite temperatures in an extended $J_1$-$J_2$ XXZ chain. The spin-current coupling between vector chirality and electric polarization offers, in principle, access to this witness through dielectric loss spectroscopy in multiferroic magnets, extending entanglement diagnostics beyond dipolar spin correlations.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a rigorous bound on the total nearest-neighbour vector chirality for periodic spin-1/2 chains: the quantum Fisher information per spin cannot exceed k+1 for any k-producible state, so exceeding this bound certifies entanglement depth of at least k+1, then demonstrates multipartite entanglement in vector-chiral correlations in an extended J1-J2 XXZ chain.
AI.motivation: Characterizing entanglement in quantum materials via experimentally accessible observables remains a central challenge. Quantum Fisher information linked to sums of one-site spin operators connects entanglement to measurable magnetic response functions, but extending this approach to local composite observables requires new entanglement bounds.
AI.method: Establish a rigorous entanglement bound for the total nearest-neighbour vector chirality of periodic spin-1/2 chains with an even number of sites, based on quantum Fisher information per spin relative to k-producible states. Combine infinite density-matrix renormalization group (iDMRG) and thermal pure quantum-state calculations to probe vector-chiral correlations at zero and finite temperatures in an extended J1-J2 XXZ chain.
AI.result: The quantum Fisher information per spin cannot exceed k+1 for any k-producible state, so exceeding this bound certifies entanglement depth of at least k+1. Multipartite entanglement encoded in vector-chiral correlations is demonstrated at both zero and finite temperatures in the extended J1-J2 XXZ chain.
AI.conclusion: Spin-current coupling between vector chirality and electric polarization offers, in principle, access to this witness through dielectric loss spectroscopy in multiferroic magnets, extending entanglement diagnostics beyond dipolar spin correlations.

title: A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem
summary: Data-driven machine learning (ML) techniques have become an essential tool in many domains of science. Their application to atomistic simulations of matter is particularly widespread and impactful. This success is due largely to the existence of a well-developed and established physics-based modeling framework, ranging from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics and statistical sampling, into which ML was integrated naturally to reshape long-standing trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and scale. Nevertheless, this integration raises both conceptual and practical challenges, from choosing between data-centric and physics-based modeling approaches to adapting established software stacks to modern hardware accelerators and ML libraries. As the field evolves rapidly, fueled in part by widespread enthusiasm but also by tangible impact, it seems appropriate to take a moment to consider the current state of the art and open challenges, and reflect on what can be done to better coordinate efforts across the community. With this goal in mind, several members of this community met in Lausanne in January 2026 at CECAM to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and the most promising scientific applications that have become possible thanks to the use of artificial intelligence in atomic-scale simulations. This strategic roadmap paper summarizes the outcomes of these discussions, suggesting some long-term goals, and some concrete actions, to establish a healthy, sustainable and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem.

AI.tldr: This strategic roadmap summarizes the outcomes of a January 2026 CECAM meeting in Lausanne on machine learning for atomistic simulation, charting the state of the art and proposing long-term goals and concrete actions to build a healthy, sustainable, and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem.
AI.motivation: ML has become widespread and impactful in atomistic simulation because it integrates naturally into an established physics-based framework—from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics and statistical sampling—reshaping long-standing trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, and scale. However, this integration raises conceptual and practical challenges, including choosing between data-centric and physics-based modeling and adapting legacy software stacks to modern hardware accelerators and ML libraries. The field's rapid, enthusiasm-driven growth motivates a pause to assess the state of the art, identify open challenges, and better coordinate community efforts.
AI.method: A community-driven strategic roadmap developed at a January 2026 CECAM meeting in Lausanne, where members of the atomistic ML community convened to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and the most promising scientific applications enabled by AI in atomic-scale simulation. The paper synthesizes these discussions into long-term goals and concrete actions.
AI.result: The paper presents a summary of community discussions covering algorithmic and modeling approaches, software and hardware infrastructure needs, and high-potential scientific applications, together with proposed long-term goals and concrete actions aimed at coordinating efforts across the community.
AI.conclusion: Establishing a healthy, sustainable, and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem requires coordinated community action, guided by the roadmap's long-term goals and concrete recommendations.

title: Operando Charge Carrier Dynamics by Intensity-Modulated Photoluminescence: From Perovskite Thin Films to Solar Cells
summary: The charge-carrier lifetime in halide perovskites often varies by orders of magnitude with the injection level, complicating the analysis of conventional time-resolved photoluminescence and comparisons of reported lifetimes. We use intensity-modulated photoluminescence spectroscopy (IMPLS) as a frequency-domain alternative. Carried out under operating conditions, it yields the lifetime at a specific injection level, e.g., one-sun-equivalent illumination. On thin films, IMPLS and steady-state photoluminescence yield comparable lifetimes. For perovskite/transport-layer stacks, the IMPLS response becomes more complex. A dedicated transfer function disentangles charge transfer from interface recombination and predicts an upper limit on the charge-carrier lifetime in the solar cell. In devices, electrical methods such as intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy (IMVS) often fail to measure the lifetime due to capacitive effects. IMPLS shows not only the same two characteristic frequencies as IMVS, but also a third one, thereby resolving the lifetime itself.

AI.tldr: Intensity-modulated photoluminescence spectroscopy (IMPLS) is presented as a frequency-domain method to extract injection-level-specific charge-carrier lifetimes in halide perovskites, outperforming conventional time-resolved techniques and electrical methods.
AI.motivation: The charge-carrier lifetime in halide perovskites varies by orders of magnitude with injection level, which complicates analysis of conventional time-resolved photoluminescence and makes comparison of reported lifetimes difficult.
AI.method: IMPLS is used as a frequency-domain alternative, applied under operating conditions (e.g., one-sun-equivalent illumination). For perovskite/transport-layer stacks, a dedicated transfer function is introduced to disentangle charge transfer from interface recombination. IMPLS is also compared with intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy (IMVS) in devices.
AI.result: On thin films, IMPLS and steady-state photoluminescence yield comparable lifetimes. For perovskite/transport-layer stacks, the transfer function predicts an upper limit on the charge-carrier lifetime in the solar cell. In devices, IMVS often fails to measure the lifetime due to capacitive effects, whereas IMPLS shows the same two characteristic frequencies as IMVS plus a third, resolving the lifetime itself.
AI.conclusion: IMPLS provides an injection-level-resolved lifetime measurement that overcomes limitations of time-resolved photoluminescence and electrical methods, enabling more reliable lifetime determination in halide perovskite films, stacks, and devices.

title: Emergent Quantum Geometric Phases in Holey Graphene
summary: In graphene and other two-dimensional materials, periodic modulations of the electron density can significantly alter the energy spectrum and transport properties. Here, we report magnetotransport measurements in encapsulated monolayer graphene with ultra-high-quality patterned periodic antidot lattices that preserve the intrinsic electronic properties of the material. This lithographically defined platform enables controlled access to commensurability and superlattice phenomena at length scales otherwise difficult to achieve. By systematically tuning the lattice dimensions, we reveal a hierarchy of classical commensurability features arising from cyclotron orbits with comparable radii that follow multiple classical trajectories, resulting in broadened resistance peaks beyond the conventional single-orbit picture. Superimposed on these features, we observe pronounced Brown-Zak oscillations arising from the quantum commensurability between the magnetic flux quantum and the unit cell of the engineered Bravais lattices. We demonstrate that the intrinsic geometric phase of our system is directly measurable and show a precise matching of the magnetic field periodicity to the lithographic periodic patterning, where moiré-like electronic spectra can be geometrically generated in single-layer graphene without the need for twist, lattice mismatch, or multilayer stacking. Our results establish nanopatterned graphene as a clean, tunable, and scalable platform for realizing and exploring moiré physics through on-demand real-space design

AI.tldr: Encapsulated monolayer graphene with ultra-high-quality patterned periodic antidot lattices enables controlled study of classical commensurability features and Brown-Zak oscillations, allowing geometric generation of moiré-like electronic spectra without twist, lattice mismatch, or multilayer stacking.
AI.motivation: Periodic modulations of electron density in graphene and other 2D materials can significantly alter energy spectrum and transport properties. The authors aim to create a clean, tunable platform that preserves intrinsic electronic properties while enabling controlled access to commensurability and superlattice phenomena at length scales otherwise difficult to achieve.
AI.method: Magnetotransport measurements in encapsulated monolayer graphene with ultra-high-quality lithographically defined patterned periodic antidot lattices; systematic tuning of lattice dimensions.
AI.result: A hierarchy of classical commensurability features arising from cyclotron orbits with comparable radii following multiple classical trajectories, producing broadened resistance peaks beyond the single-orbit picture; superimposed pronounced Brown-Zak oscillations from quantum commensurability between the magnetic flux quantum and the engineered Bravais lattice unit cell; direct measurement of intrinsic geometric phase; precise matching of magnetic field periodicity to lithographic periodic patterning.
AI.conclusion: Nanopatterned graphene is established as a clean, tunable, and scalable platform for realizing and exploring moiré physics through on-demand real-space design, geometrically generating moiré-like electronic spectra in single-layer graphene without twist, lattice mismatch, or multilayer stacking.

title: An electromechanically coupled multiphase-field model with generalized kinetic relations for ferroelectrics
summary: Classical phase-field models typically use the Allen--Cahn evolution law to model interface motion as a consequence of energy-gradient descent. This implies a linear kinetic relation between the velocity of an interface (e.g., a domain wall in a ferroelectric) and its driving force. When nonlinear kinetic relations are to be modeled, as commonly found in ferroelectric ceramics, an alternative evolution law and hence an alternative model is needed. Here, we propose an electromechanically (stress-driven) coupled multiphase-field framework with a general kinetic formulation, which integrates a prescribed kinetic relation directly into the evolution law. We show that this model correctly evolves domain walls with the assigned nonlinear kinetics, e.g., of mixed exponential-power law type, following the so-called Merz--Stadler law. The multiphase formulation further enables distinct kinetic relations and interfacial energies to be assigned to different order-parameter pairs, which reflects the distinguishable properties of the different types of ferroelectric domain walls. The proposed framework is broadly applicable for simulating kinetic relations in materials with applications beyond ferroelectrics.

AI.tldr: A stress-driven coupled multiphase-field framework embeds a prescribed (possibly nonlinear) kinetic relation directly into the evolution law, enabling correct simulation of ferroelectric domain-wall motion, including Merz–Stadler-type mixed exponential–power kinetics, with distinct kinetics and interfacial energies assignable to different order-parameter pairs.
AI.motivation: Classical phase-field models rely on the Allen–Cahn evolution law, which imposes a linear kinetic relation between interface velocity and driving force. Ferroelectric ceramics, however, commonly exhibit nonlinear kinetic relations, so an alternative evolution law and model are required.
AI.method: The authors propose an electromechanically coupled (stress-driven) multiphase-field framework with a general kinetic formulation that integrates a prescribed kinetic relation directly into the evolution law. The multiphase formulation allows different kinetic relations and interfacial energies to be assigned to different order-parameter pairs.
AI.result: The model correctly evolves domain walls according to the assigned nonlinear kinetics, including a mixed exponential–power law following the Merz–Stadler law. It also captures the distinguishable properties of different ferroelectric domain-wall types via pair-specific kinetics and energies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables simulation of general kinetic relations in ferroelectric domain-wall motion and is broadly applicable to other materials beyond ferroelectrics.

title: The Hidden Topology of Network Entanglement
summary: Topology and geometry are inseparable in physical networks. Here we show that, after factoring out the topology-dependent number of eligible edge pairs, exchangeability makes the mean crossing propensity of those pairs exactly graph independent while preserving topology in fluctuations. We derive a microscopic, parameter-free theory for the response when topology and geometry are coupled. Synthetic and real three-dimensional networks confirm that structure hidden from the normalized mean survives in correlations that determine response.

AI.tldr: After factoring out the topology-dependent number of eligible edge pairs, exchangeability makes the mean crossing propensity exactly graph-independent while topology persists in fluctuations, yielding a parameter-free microscopic theory for response in coupled topology-geometry networks.
AI.motivation: Topology and geometry are inseparable in physical networks, yet the standard normalized mean of edge-pair crossing propensity obscures structural information. The paper seeks a framework that decouples the graph-independent mean from topology-dependent behavior.
AI.method: Factor out the topology-dependent count of eligible edge pairs, then apply exchangeability to show the mean crossing propensity becomes exactly graph-independent while topology is retained in fluctuations. Derive a microscopic, parameter-free theory for the response under coupled topology and geometry.
AI.result: Synthetic and real three-dimensional networks confirm that structure hidden from the normalized mean survives in correlations that govern the network's response.
AI.conclusion: Topological information is encoded in fluctuations/correlations rather than the normalized mean; these correlations determine physical response, motivating a parameter-free microscopic description of coupled topology-geometry networks.

title: Enabling Domain-Specific Atomistic Models: A Machine Learning Potential for the Solid Acid Family
summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained across the periodic table have made atomistic simulation broadly accessible, and specializing them to a single compound class is widely expected to improve accuracy. Yet examples remain scarce, and fewer still surpass universal models in speed or reach a higher level of electronic-structure theory. Here we present a potential that is universal within the class of water-free solid-state hydrogen-bond network mediated proton conductors rather than across chemistry and a database of 4.4 million first-principles configurations spanning 55 materials. It surpasses leading general-purpose potentials across this domain, recovering measured activation energies and the ordering of anion rotational dynamics that those models miss; agreement on static structure does not imply agreement on transport. Accuracy falls for compositions far from the training set but stays competitive for close structural relatives, and a higher level of electronic-structure theory is reached with a few hundred additional configurations per material. We further introduce a compact variant carrying a fifth of the parameters, faster still and yet more accurate than every general-purpose model tested. It sustains more than a quarter of a million atoms on a single graphics processor, placing grain boundaries and the transition into the highly conducting phase within reach, and making a quantum treatment of the protons affordable. Reference accuracy and accessible system size thus become largely independent, offering a template for other compound classes.

AI.motivation: While machine-learned interatomic potentials trained across the periodic table have made atomistic simulation broadly accessible, specializing them to a single compound class is widely expected to improve accuracy, yet examples remain scarce. Fewer still surpass universal models in speed or reach a higher level of electronic-structure theory.
AI.method: The authors construct a potential that is universal within the class of water-free solid-state hydrogen-bond network mediated proton conductors (not across all chemistry), trained on a database of 4.4 million first-principles configurations spanning 55 materials. They also introduce a compact variant with one-fifth of the parameters. Accuracy is assessed via measured activation energies, anion rotational dynamics ordering, and static structure, with a higher level of electronic-structure theory reached using a few hundred additional configurations per material.
