title: Varying A-site radius and size disorder to tune magnetic ordering in compositionally complex perovskite oxides
summary: A long standing goal of magnetochemists is to be able to control ordering temperatures through compositional engineering. Here we report the synthesis of a perovskite oxide with twelve cations accommodated within a single phase solid solution, AM7O$_3$, A = La$_{\frac{1}{5}}$Sm$_{\frac{1}{5}}$Gd$_{\frac{1}{5}}$Nd$_{\frac{1}{5}}$Dy$_{\frac{1}{5}}$ (A5), and M7 = Ti$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Cr$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Mn$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Fe$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Co$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Ni$_{\frac{1}{7}}$Cu$_{\frac{1}{7}}$. Bulk magnetometry measurements for A5M7O$_3$, as well as for A = La, Gd and La$_{\frac{1}{2}}$Gd$_{\frac{1}{2}}$, show that all these compounds magnetically order as ferrimagnets between 89 and 115 K. We find that the magnetic properties are influenced by considering a combination of the size disorder parameter alongside the A-site cationic radii and valence electrons.

AI.tldr: A single-phase perovskite oxide accommodating twelve cations (A5M7O3) was synthesized and shown to order ferrimagnetically between 89 and 115 K.
AI.motivation: Magnetochemists have long sought to control magnetic ordering temperatures via compositional engineering, motivating the design of highly complex, multi-cation single-phase oxides.
AI.method: Synthesis of a perovskite oxide AM7O3 with A = La1/5Sm1/5Gd1/5Nd1/5Dy1/5 (A5) and M7 = Ti1/7Cr1/7Mn1/7Fe1/7Co1/7Ni1/7Cu1/7, alongside reference compounds with A = La, Gd, and La1/2Gd1/2, characterized by bulk magnetometry.
AI.result: All synthesized compounds magnetically order as ferrimagnets with ordering temperatures between 89 and 115 K. Magnetic properties correlate with a combination of the size disorder parameter, A-site cationic radii, and valence electron count.
AI.conclusion: High-entropy, multi-cation perovskite oxides can be realized as single phases with tunable ferrimagnetic ordering temperatures, where size disorder, cation radii, and valence electrons together govern magnetic behavior, offering a route to compositional control of magnetism.

title: Anisotropic wavevector-dependent damping of thickness-quantized magnons
summary: Magnon damping is a key factor governing spin-wave transport and nonlinear dynamics of multimode magnon systems. However, many descriptions rely on the assumption of an effective mode-independent parameter, which can mask wavelength-dependent relaxation processes that depend on propagation geometry and mode profile. Here, we employ high-resolution parametric-instability spectroscopy to probe thickness-quantized spin waves with wavelengths down to about a hundred nanometers in micrometer-thick yttrium iron garnet films. The instability threshold exhibits a regular sawtooth dependence on the magnetic field, arising from switching between discrete thickness modes. Comparison with dipole--exchange theory reveals anisotropic wavevector-dependent damping that increases with mode number and depends differently on the in-plane and out-of-plane wavevector components.

AI.tldr: Magnon damping is studied in thick YIG films using parametric-instability spectroscopy; the instability threshold shows sawtooth field dependence from discrete thickness modes, revealing anisotropic wavevector-dependent damping that grows with mode number.
AI.motivation: Many magnon damping descriptions assume a mode-independent effective parameter, masking wavelength-dependent relaxation processes tied to propagation geometry and mode profile. The paper aims to resolve such mode- and wavevector-resolved damping.
AI.method: High-resolution parametric-instability spectroscopy probes thickness-quantized spin waves with wavelengths down to ~100 nm in micrometer-thick yttrium iron garnet films. Results are compared with dipole-exchange theory.
AI.result: The instability threshold exhibits a regular sawtooth dependence on magnetic field, caused by switching between discrete thickness modes. The comparison reveals anisotropic, wavevector-dependent damping that increases with mode number and depends differently on in-plane versus out-of-plane wavevector components.
AI.conclusion: Magnon damping is not a single mode-independent parameter but is anisotropic and mode-dependent, with distinct in-plane and out-of-plane wavevector contributions, as resolved in thick YIG films.

title: Smart Machine Learning for Solving the Full Electron-Nuclear Schrödinger Equation with a Quantum-Chemically Inspired Wavefunction Ansatz
summary: Directly solving the full electron-nuclear Schrödinger equation remains one of the grand challenges in quantum mechanics. Here, we propose a quantum-chemically motivated orbital-based neural network wavefunction ansatz with explicit many-body electron-electron correlation terms, with parameters depending on the entire electron-nuclear configuration, enabling an accurate description of strongly correlated and/or multi-reference electronic structures by a single Slater-determinant across a broad nuclear configuration space. To train this wavefunction, we further develop an efficient hybrid optimization strategy that combines the variational Monte Carlo technique with local-energy constraints, mitigating the intrinsic sampling bias of the former and considerably reducing the statistical error. These advances are embedded in a unified neural network framework, Schrödinger, enabling the determination of globally accurate potential energy surfaces with a single training for systems ranging from strongly correlated diatomic molecules, triatomic reactions containing conical intersections, to polyatomic multi-reference molecules. This work offers a practical machine-learning tool for solving the electron-nuclear Schrödinger equation and capturing full quantum effects beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.

AI.tldr: The authors propose an orbital-based neural network wavefunction ansatz with explicit many-body electron-electron correlation terms and nuclear-configuration-dependent parameters, trained via a hybrid variational Monte Carlo plus local-energy-constraint optimization, to obtain globally accurate potential energy surfaces for strongly correlated, multi-reference, and non-Born-Oppenheimer systems.
AI.motivation: Directly solving the full electron-nuclear Schrödinger equation remains a grand challenge. Existing neural network wavefunctions struggle to describe strongly correlated and multi-reference electronic structures accurately with a single Slater determinant, and variational Monte Carlo suffers from intrinsic sampling bias and large statistical error.
AI.method: A quantum-chemically motivated orbital-based neural network wavefunction ansatz with explicit many-body electron-electron correlation terms, whose parameters depend on the entire electron-nuclear configuration, allowing a single Slater determinant to capture strongly correlated and multi-reference electronic structures across broad nuclear configuration space. Training uses a hybrid optimization strategy combining variational Monte Carlo with local-energy constraints. These components are integrated into a unified neural network framework, Schrödinger.
AI.result: The framework yields globally accurate potential energy surfaces from a single training for systems including strongly correlated diatomic molecules, triatomic reactions with conical intersections, and polyatomic multi-reference molecules. The hybrid optimization mitigates sampling bias and considerably reduces statistical error.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a practical machine-learning tool for solving the electron-nuclear Schrödinger equation and capturing full quantum effects beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.

title: CYNAR: a trajectory-based estimator of entropy production
summary: Inferring the entropy production rate $σ$ from recorded trajectories is a key challenge in stochastic thermodynamics. In experiments, the forces governing the dynamics are usually unknown and often only some of the system's degrees of freedom can be observed. Building on a recently introduced method [I. Di Terlizzi, Phys. Rev. Lett. 135, 237101 (2025)], we develop and validate CYNAR (computation yields nonequilibrium analysis and reconstruction), a pipeline that estimates $σ$ from trajectories. It exploits a kinetic decomposition of $σ$ into a traffic term ${\cal T}$, inferred from the short-time curvature of correlation functions, and an inflow rate ${\cal G}$, computed from the steady-state score, i.e., the gradient of the log-density. We show that the same decomposition, evaluated on any subset of observed coordinates, always bounds $σ$ from below, for any diffusion tensor and without knowledge of the hidden degrees of freedom. We then compare CYNAR with a more standard approach that estimates $σ$ from steady-state probability currents, on four systems of increasing complexity. CYNAR proves to be more reliable, with no detectable bias close to equilibrium, weak dependence on spatial discretization, and marked robustness to measurement noise. It is also readily applicable to high-dimensional systems, where the traffic alone provides a lower bound close to $σ$, and remains informative under partial observation, including cases where the flux-based estimate vanishes identically. CYNAR is provided as an open-source Python package.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CYNAR, a pipeline that estimates the entropy production rate σ from recorded trajectories by decomposing σ into a traffic term (inferred from short-time curvature of correlation functions) and an inflow rate (from the steady-state score), validated against a flux-based method across four systems.
AI.motivation: Inferring the entropy production rate from trajectories is a key challenge in stochastic thermodynamics, but in experiments the governing forces are usually unknown and often only a subset of degrees of freedom can be observed, complicating standard estimation approaches.
AI.method: Building on a recently introduced method, CYNAR exploits a kinetic decomposition of σ into a traffic term T (inferred from the short-time curvature of correlation functions) and an inflow rate G (computed from the steady-state score, i.e., the gradient of the log-density). The same decomposition evaluated on any subset of observed coordinates always bounds σ from below, for any diffusion tensor and without knowledge of hidden degrees of freedom. CYNAR is compared with a standard approach that estimates σ from steady-state probability currents on four systems of increasing complexity.
AI.result: CYNAR proves more reliable, with no detectable bias close to equilibrium, weak dependence on spatial discretization, and marked robustness to measurement noise. It is readily applicable to high-dimensional systems, where the traffic alone gives a lower bound close to σ, and remains informative under partial observation, including cases where the flux-based estimate vanishes identically.
AI.conclusion: CYNAR offers a robust and broadly applicable pipeline for estimating entropy production from trajectories, overcoming limitations of flux-based methods, and is released as an open-source Python package.

title: Dense and porous phase transition study of SEI formation using phase-field method
comment: It has 7 figures and 1 supplementary paper
summary: The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is essential for the long-term stability of batteries because it influences the reactions between the electrode and electrolyte. Despite previous studies, the SEI evolution from dense to porous phases remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the SoC-dependent evolution of the SEI using a phase-field framework under open-circuit conditions. Spatially correlated noise is introduced to describe stochastic transport perturbations, and the dense-to-porous transition time is evaluated from the evolution of interface roughness arising from the competition between noise-induced transport and surface relaxation. The simulations reveal three distinct roughness evolution regimes. The predicted transition time generally increases from approximately one month at 20% SoC to more than seven months at 80% SoC, with a pronounced change between 55% and 60%. This change corresponds to the graphite SoC-OCV relation, which controls the interfacial Li0 radical concentration through the Nernst condition. Under dynamic SoC conditions caused by irreversible capacity loss, the transition behavior changes as the SoC evolves during storage. These results show that the SoC-OCV relation is central to determining SEI phase stability and the dense-to-porous transition time under open-circuit storage.

AI.tldr: A phase-field study with spatially correlated noise reveals three roughness evolution regimes in the SEI and predicts a dense-to-porous transition time that grows from ~1 month at 20% SoC to >7 months at 80% SoC, with a sharp change between 55% and 60% SoC governed by the graphite SoC-OCV relation.
AI.motivation: The SEI is critical for battery long-term stability, yet its evolution from a dense to a porous phase remains poorly understood. Prior work has not resolved how state of charge (SoC) governs this transition, so a mechanism linking SoC, interfacial chemistry, and SEI phase stability under open-circuit storage is needed.
AI.method: A phase-field framework is used to model SoC-dependent SEI evolution under open-circuit conditions. Spatially correlated noise is introduced to represent stochastic transport perturbations. The dense-to-porous transition time is extracted from the evolution of interfacial roughness, which arises from competition between noise-induced transport and surface relaxation. The interfacial Li0 radical concentration is linked to the graphite SoC-OCV relation via the Nernst condition, and dynamic SoC conditions from irreversible capacity loss are also simulated.
AI.result: Three distinct roughness evolution regimes are identified. The predicted transition time increases from about one month at 20% SoC to more than seven months at 80% SoC, with a pronounced change between 55% and 60% SoC. This change tracks the graphite SoC-OCV relation, which controls interfacial Li0 radical concentration through the Nernst condition. Under dynamic SoC from irreversible capacity loss, the transition behavior shifts as SoC evolves during storage.
AI.conclusion: The SoC-OCV relation is central to determining SEI phase stability and the dense-to-porous transition time during open-circuit storage, providing a mechanistic basis for predicting SEI evolution and calendar aging.

title: Elasticity of polycrystalline davemaoite constrains its grain size in the lower mantle
summary: Earth's lower mantle hosts large low shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) beneath Africa and the Pacific, but their origin remains debated. Davemaoite, a major lower-mantle mineral, has been proposed as a contributor to these anomalies; however, its experimentally measured shear modulus is approximately 30% lower than first-principles predictions, a longstanding discrepancy between theory and experiment. Here, using million-atom machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations, we show that nanoscale grain-boundary disorder, invisible to conventional x-ray diffraction, can reconcile this gap. Introducing 5.8 vol% disordered regions reduces the shear and bulk moduli by 37% and 12%, respectively. This shear-selective softening can reproduce LLSVP-like seismic anomalies in basalt-rich assemblages, but only at disorder levels corresponding to grain sizes smaller than those expected in the lower mantle. Combining the disorder-elasticity relationship with seismic constraints, we derive a minimum davemaoite grain size of approximately 100 nm. This limit is consistent with mantle grain growth models and with attenuation-based evidence for coarse-grained LLSVPs.

AI.tldr: Nanoscale grain-boundary disorder in davemaoite can explain the shear-modulus discrepancy between experiments and theory, but reproducing LLSVP-like anomalies requires unrealistically small grains. Combining disorder-elasticity relations with seismic constraints yields a minimum davemaoite grain size of ~100 nm.
AI.motivation: Earth's lower mantle contains large low shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) whose origin is debated. Davemaoite, a major lower-mantle mineral, is a proposed contributor, but its measured shear modulus is ~30% lower than first-principles predictions—a longstanding theory-experiment discrepancy that must be resolved to assess its role in LLSVPs.
AI.method: Million-atom machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations are used to test whether nanoscale grain-boundary disorder (undetectable by conventional x-ray diffraction) can account for the moduli gap. The effect of introducing ~5.8 vol% disordered regions on shear and bulk moduli is quantified, and the disorder-elasticity relationship is combined with seismic constraints.
AI.result: Adding 5.8 vol% disordered regions reduces shear and bulk moduli by 37% and 12%, respectively—a shear-selective softening. This softening reproduces LLSVP-like seismic anomalies in basalt-rich assemblages, but only for disorder levels corresponding to grain sizes smaller than those expected in the lower mantle. Combining disorder-elasticity relations with seismic constraints gives a minimum davemaoite grain size of ~100 nm.
AI.conclusion: Grain-boundary disorder can reconcile the theory-experiment shear-modulus discrepancy, but LLSVP-like anomalies require grains finer than expected, implying that disorder alone cannot explain LLSVPs at realistic grain sizes. The derived ~100 nm minimum grain size is consistent with mantle grain growth models and attenuation-based evidence for coarse-grained LLSVPs.

title: A transferable full-band Monte Carlo framework for complex alloy avalanche photodiodes
summary: We present a physics-based multiscale full-band Monte Carlo framework for modeling avalanche multiplication and excess noise in complex alloy avalanche photodiodes (APDs), demonstrated on Al$_{0.7}$InAsSb as a representative quaternary system. The framework links atomistic material structure to device-level avalanche statistics: an environment-dependent $sp^3d^5s^\ast$ tight-binding calculation resolves the full conduction- and valence-band structure of the random- or digital-alloy configuration -- including $Γ$, X, and L valley ordering, non-parabolicity, anisotropy, and spin-orbit-induced valence-band splitting -- and supplies the band-structure inputs for stochastic high-field transport. A central element of the framework is a physics-derived treatment of alloy-disorder scattering, in which the quaternary disorder potential is constructed from atomic valence differences, covalent radii, and Thomas--Fermi screening through a composition-weighted decomposition into binary contributions, complemented by composition-interpolated polar-optical, acoustic, intervalley-phonon, impurity, and impact-ionization models. Because every material-dependent input is generated from the atomic composition and configuration by the same well-defined procedure, the framework transfers without structural modification to arbitrary zinc-blende ternary and quaternary alloys. Applied to a \SI{1}{\micro\meter} Al$_{0.7}$InAsSb p-i-n APD, the framework reproduces the measured gain and excess-noise characteristics with only the impact-ionization softness parameters calibrated. The approach provides a documented, reproducible route for analyzing and designing complex alloy APDs in which band structure, disorder, and scattering physics jointly determine gain and ionization statistics.

AI.tldr: A physics-based multiscale full-band Monte Carlo framework links atomistic tight-binding band structure to device-level avalanche statistics in complex alloy APDs, validated on AlInAsSb p-i-n diodes.
AI.motivation: Complex quaternary alloy APDs require predictive modeling of avalanche multiplication and excess noise, but existing approaches struggle to connect atomistic material structure, alloy disorder, and scattering physics to device-level gain and ionization statistics.
AI.method: An environment-dependent sp3d5s* tight-binding calculation resolves the full band structure of random- or digital-alloy configurations (Γ, X, L ordering, non-parabolicity, anisotropy, spin-orbit splitting) and feeds a stochastic full-band Monte Carlo high-field transport model. Alloy-disorder scattering is physics-derived from atomic valence differences, covalent radii, and Thomas-Fermi screening via composition-weighted binary decomposition, complemented by composition-interpolated polar-optical, acoustic, intervalley-phonon, impurity, and impact-ionization models; all inputs are generated from atomic composition/configuration, enabling transfer to arbitrary zinc-blende ternaries and quaternaries.
AI.result: Applied to a 1 µm Al0.7InAsSb p-i-n APD, the framework reproduces measured gain and excess-noise characteristics with only the impact-ionization softness parameters calibrated.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a documented, reproducible route for analyzing and designing complex alloy APDs where band structure, disorder, and scattering jointly govern gain and ionization statistics.

title: Magnetization relaxation of interacting chains of nanomagnets
summary: We investigate the magnetization dynamics crossover from single-particle to collective behavior in a one-dimensional chain of dipolar-coupled nanomagnets with uniaxial anisotropy. Using both an intermediate-to-high damping (IHD) analytical approach based on Langer's theory and time-quantified Monte Carlo (TQMC) simulations, we derive and validate semi-analytical expressions for the relaxation rate and the magnetization relaxation curves. Our main results include: (i) a closed-form expression for the relaxation rate accounting for (weak) dipolar interactions, (ii) a two-exponential semi-analytical formula for the magnetization dynamics $m(t)$ of an interacting chain, and (iii) a systematic comparison with TQMC simulations, showing good agreement for a wide range of parameters. The analysis reveals a field-controlled crossover from uniform (macrospin-like) reversal to edge-nucleation propagation, driven by the spatial inhomogeneity of dipolar stabilization. The derived expressions provide a computationally efficient framework for predicting the relaxation behavior of dipolar-coupled nanomagnetic assemblies.

AI.tldr: The paper derives semi-analytical expressions for the relaxation rate and magnetization dynamics of a 1D dipolar-coupled nanomagnet chain, validated by Monte Carlo simulations, revealing a field-controlled crossover from uniform macrospin-like reversal to edge-nucleation propagation.
AI.motivation: Understanding the crossover from single-particle to collective magnetization behavior in dipolar-coupled nanomagnet assemblies is important, but computationally efficient predictive models for their relaxation behavior are lacking.
AI.method: Intermediate-to-high damping (IHD) analytical approach based on Langer's theory combined with time-quantified Monte Carlo (TQMC) simulations, applied to a 1D chain of dipolar-coupled nanomagnets with uniaxial anisotropy.
AI.result: (i) A closed-form relaxation rate expression incorporating weak dipolar interactions; (ii) a two-exponential semi-analytical formula for the interacting chain's m(t); (iii) good agreement with TQMC simulations over a wide parameter range. A field-controlled crossover from uniform macrospin-like reversal to edge-nucleation propagation emerges, driven by spatial inhomogeneity of dipolar stabilization.
AI.conclusion: The derived expressions offer a computationally efficient framework for predicting the relaxation behavior of dipolar-coupled nanomagnetic assemblies.

title: Minimizing capture time with many small traps in heterogeneous media
summary: We study the problem of optimally placing a large number of small absorbing traps to minimize the mean first-passage time (MFPT) of particles diffusing in a heterogeneous medium with space-dependent diffusivity $D(x)$ and prescribed initial particle distribution $ω(x)$. In two and three dimensions we identify two distinct regimes, depending on how strongly the trap ensemble depletes the particles. In the weak trapping regime (fewer traps) the optimal trap density $ρ$ is the arithmetic average $ρ= \frac12(μ+ω)$ of the normalized inverse diffusivity $μ\propto 1/D$ and the initial particle distribution $ω$. In the strong trapping regime (more traps), it is proportional to their geometric average, $ρ\propto \sqrt{μω}$. We revisit the classical Green's function approach and show that it applies to weak trapping only; in 2D this requires the trap size to be exponentially small in the number of traps, so that most applications of interest fall in the strong trapping regime instead. We therefore develop a homogenization approach that captures both regimes. A special choice of initial particle distribution is $ω\propto 1/D$, which corresponds to the equilibrium particle distribution in the absence of traps according to the Itô interpretation. In this case we show that the optimal trap distribution is the stationary particle distribution itself, regardless of the trapping strength, and this makes the MFPT constant throughout the domain; the same trap distribution also minimizes the worst-case capture time. Finally, in one dimension we find instead $ρ\propto\left(μω\right) ^{1/3}$, and a similar analysis covers space-dependent drift and thin domains of variable cross-section. Direct numerical optimization confirms the analytical results.

AI.tldr: Optimal trap placement to minimize MFPT in heterogeneous media splits into weak (arithmetic-average density) and strong (geometric-average density) trapping regimes; a homogenization approach captures both, with special cases in 1D and equilibrium initial distributions.
AI.motivation: Placing many small absorbing traps optimally to minimize the mean first-passage time (MFPT) of diffusing particles is important in heterogeneous media where diffusivity D(x) and initial particle distribution ω(x) vary in space. Existing classical Green's function approaches may not cover all relevant regimes.
AI.method: The authors revisit the classical Green's function approach and develop a homogenization approach that captures both weak and strong trapping regimes. They analyze 2D and 3D cases, plus 1D, and extend the analysis to space-dependent drift and thin domains of variable cross-section. Direct numerical optimization is used for confirmation.
AI.result: In weak trapping, optimal trap density ρ equals the arithmetic average ρ = ½(μ + ω) of normalized inverse diffusivity μ ∝ 1/D and initial distribution ω. In strong trapping, ρ ∝ √(μω) (geometric average). The Green's function approach applies only to weak trapping; in 2D this requires exponentially small trap size in the number of traps, so most applications fall in the strong trapping regime. For ω ∝ 1/D (equilibrium under Itô interpretation), the optimal trap distribution equals the stationary particle distribution regardless of trapping strength, making MFPT constant and minimizing worst-case capture time. In 1D, ρ ∝ (μω)^{1/3}.
AI.conclusion: The optimal trap distribution depends on trapping strength: arithmetic average (weak), geometric average (strong), or (μω)^{1/3} in 1D. The homogenization approach unifies both regimes, and numerical optimization confirms the analytical predictions. Equilibrium initial distributions yield a self-consistent optimal trap density that equalizes MFPT.

title: Polymorph-Tunable Spin Texture and Excitonic Structures in Monolayer WSi2P4
summary: Two-dimensional semiconductors that simultaneously possess a direct band gap and strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) are highly attractive for quantum optoelectronics. Using first-principles GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) calculations, we show that monolayer WSi2P4-an experimentally accessible member of the MSi2X4 family-hosts a direct K-valley gap together with strong SOC. Its three competing polymorphs (alpha, beta and gamma) are all direct-gap semiconductors and are kinetically locked behind 1.3 eV migration barriers. The sigma_h mirror plane of the D3h of alpha and gamma phases enforces a persistent spin texture across the Brillouin zone, weakly modulated near gamma by interband SOC mixing, whereas the polar beta phase (C3v) exhibits Rashba spin splitting. SOC splits the doubly-degenerate lowest bright exciton into dark states and splits the original absorption peak into two peaks (A and B), whose relative brightness is governed by the K-valley conduction-band splitting. alpha-WSi2P4 displays the brightest Peak A because a tiny band crossing of opposite-spin branches can open a spin-allowed radiative channel. These results establish the MSi2P4 family as a phase-tunable platform for the cooperative engineering of spin texture, band splitting, and excitonic brightness within a single material system.

AI.tldr: Monolayer WSi2P4 (an MSi2X4 family member) is shown via GW-BSE to be a direct-gap, strong-SOC 2D semiconductor whose three polymorphs (alpha, beta, gamma) enable tunable spin texture and excitonic brightness.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional semiconductors combining a direct band gap with strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) are highly desirable for quantum optoelectronics, motivating the search for experimentally accessible materials that unify these properties.
AI.method: First-principles GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) calculations, supplemented by analysis of migration barriers, symmetry (D3h vs C3v point groups), spin texture, interband SOC mixing, and exciton fine structure.
AI.result: All three polymorphs (alpha, beta, gamma) are direct-gap semiconductors kinetically locked behind 1.3 eV migration barriers. The sigma_h mirror plane of D3h in alpha and gamma enforces a persistent spin texture across the Brillouin zone, weakly modulated near gamma by interband SOC mixing, while polar beta (C3v) shows Rashba spin splitting. SOC splits the doubly-degenerate lowest bright exciton into dark states and the absorption peak into A and B peaks, with relative brightness governed by K-valley conduction-band splitting. alpha-WSi2P4 has the brightest Peak A due to a tiny opposite-spin band crossing opening a spin-allowed radiative channel.
AI.conclusion: The MSi2P4 family constitutes a phase-tunable platform for cooperative engineering of spin texture, band splitting, and excitonic brightness within a single material system.

title: Qantum Well Resonant Tunneling Diode Probe of Correlated States in Twisted Bilayer MoS$_2$
summary: Moiré superlattices formed in transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer a versatile platform for exploring emergent quantum phases arising from strong electronic correlations. In this work, we develop a new experimental platform, the quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD), to probe the electronic landscape of $\approx 57^\circ$ twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ (tMoS$_2$). By measuring the differential conductance ($dI/dV_{\text{Probe}}$) as a function of filling factor $ν$ and displacement field $D$, we observe a robust integer correlated insulating state at $ν= 1$ that persists across the measured displacement field range. Furthermore, we identify a displacement-field-induced fractional insulating state at $ν= 3/4$ for $D < -75$~mV/nm. Temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent measurements characterize this $ν= 3/4$ state as a potential generalized Wigner crystal. These correlated states are also observed in another device with a similar twist angle ($\approx 56.5^\circ$). Our results provide direct evidence of correlated states in near-AB-stacked tMoS$_2$ and establish QWRTD as a powerful experimental tool for investigating strong correlations and topology in van der Waals heterostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum well resonant tunneling diode (QWRTD) platform to probe correlated electronic states in ~57° twisted bilayer MoS2, revealing a robust ν=1 integer correlated insulator and a displacement-field-induced ν=3/4 fractional insulator (a potential generalized Wigner crystal).
AI.motivation: Moiré superlattices in transition metal dichalcogenides provide a platform for studying strong electronic correlations and emergent quantum phases, motivating the need for new experimental tools that can probe the electronic landscape of such systems.
AI.method: A QWRTD device is used to measure differential conductance (dI/dV_Probe) as a function of filling factor ν and displacement field D in ≈57° twisted bilayer MoS2, complemented by temperature- and magnetic-field-dependent measurements on a second device with a similar twist angle (≈56.5°).
AI.result: A robust integer correlated insulating state at ν=1 persists across the measured displacement field range, and a displacement-field-induced fractional insulating state at ν=3/4 appears for D < −75 mV/nm. The ν=3/4 state is characterized as a potential generalized Wigner crystal, and both correlated states are reproduced in the second device.
AI.conclusion: The results provide direct evidence of correlated states in near-AB-stacked twisted bilayer MoS2 and establish QWRTD as a powerful tool for investigating strong correlations and topology in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Multi-Branch Transport in a Back-gated WS$_2$ Transistor at Deep-Cryogenic Temperature
summary: Two-dimensional materials are promising candidates for electronic applications beyond the operating limits of conventional semiconductor technologies. Within this class, transition-metal dichalcogenides offer attractive properties for field-effect transistor operation, with tungsten disulphide (WS$_2$) emerging as a particularly promising material for operation at cryogenic temperatures. Here, we investigate the electrical performance of a back-gated multilayer WS$_2$ transistor at deep cryogenic temperature, down to 20 mK. The device remains strongly gate-tunable throughout the cryogenic regime, with an effective on/off current ratio exceeding $10^{5}$. Most notably, the low-temperature turn-on characteristics exhibit reproducible shoulder-like features, which we describe using a phenomenological model comprising multiple effective conduction branches operating in parallel.

AI.tldr: A back-gated multilayer WS2 transistor is electrically characterized down to 20 mK, showing strong gate tunability, an on/off ratio above 10^5, and reproducible shoulder-like turn-on features modeled as multiple parallel conduction branches.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional materials, particularly transition-metal dichalcogenides such as WS2, are promising for electronics beyond conventional semiconductor limits, and WS2 is attractive for cryogenic field-effect transistor operation. However, the electrical behavior of WS2 devices at deep cryogenic temperatures remains underexplored.
AI.method: The electrical performance of a back-gated multilayer WS2 field-effect transistor was measured at deep cryogenic temperatures down to 20 mK. The low-temperature turn-on characteristics were analyzed with a phenomenological model composed of multiple effective conduction branches operating in parallel.
AI.result: The device remains strongly gate-tunable throughout the cryogenic regime, with an effective on/off current ratio exceeding 10^5. Reproducible shoulder-like features appear in the low-temperature turn-on characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Multilayer WS2 transistors are viable for deep cryogenic operation, and their low-temperature turn-on behavior can be described by multiple parallel effective conduction branches, offering a phenomenological framework for interpreting such cryogenic transport features.

title: Many-body topology in parity-preserving tensor networks
summary: Planar parity-preserving tensor networks (ppTNs) admit a fermionic formulation in which the Gaussian, efficiently contractible limit is deformed by local interactions. We investigate how many-body methods can be used to analyze such contractions in a minimal two-parameter ppTN. Its contraction is simultaneously an interacting fermionic partition function, a loop gas, a deformed toric-code norm, and a quartic Ising model, allowing the same phase diagram to be approached with complementary tools. At its center lies a `topological island', characterized beyond the Gaussian limit by a boundary-twist $\mathbb Z_2$ indicator that reduces to Chern-number parity and admits a loop-winding interpretation under duality. Fermionic perturbation theory predicts the interacting phase boundaries, tensor-network numerics establish their critical behavior, and the loop and spin descriptions reveal a self-dual line with a $c=1$ four-state-Potts multicritical fixed point.

AI.tldr: A minimal two-parameter planar parity-preserving tensor network is studied via four complementary descriptions, revealing a topological island, a Z2 boundary-twist indicator, and a self-dual line with a c=1 four-state-Potts multicritical point.
AI.motivation: Planar parity-preserving tensor networks have a fermionic formulation whose Gaussian, efficiently contractible limit is deformed by local interactions, and it is unclear how many-body methods can analyze such contractions beyond the Gaussian regime.
AI.method: The contraction of a minimal two-parameter ppTN is mapped to several equivalent models: an interacting fermionic partition function, a loop gas, a deformed toric-code norm, and a quartic Ising model. These are analyzed with fermionic perturbation theory, tensor-network numerics, and loop/spin dual descriptions, using a boundary-twist Z2 indicator that reduces to Chern-number parity and has a loop-winding interpretation under duality.
AI.result: Fermionic perturbation theory predicts the interacting phase boundaries; tensor-network numerics establish their critical behavior; the loop and spin descriptions reveal a self-dual line hosting a c=1 four-state-Potts multicritical fixed point. A central 'topological island' is characterized beyond the Gaussian limit.
AI.conclusion: The equivalence of interacting fermionic, loop-gas, deformed toric-code, and quartic Ising descriptions allows the same phase diagram to be accessed with complementary tools, extending the characterization of topological order beyond the Gaussian contraction limit.

title: Defect Dynamics and Isomer Quenching in $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ Crystals
summary: Thorium-229 doped calcium fluoride ($^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$) is a leading candidate for a solid-state nuclear clock, owing to the unusually low energy of the $^{229}$Th isomer transition at 8.3557\,eV and the very high banggap of CaF$_2$ around 12\,eV. Here we report a temperature-dependent study of $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ luminescence, covering radioluminescence, photoluminescence, thermoluminescence, and afterglow. Using synchrotron x-ray excitation together with a cryo-vacuum system, we resolve the thermal quenching of the self-trapped exciton (STE) scintillation into its triplet and singlet components, identify eleven thermoluminescence glow peaks together with their associated emission bands, and separate the temperature-dependent components that make up the long-lived afterglow. The trap depths obtained in this way are closely correlated with the temperature dependence of x-ray-induced isomer quenching, including the enhanced isomer yield near \SI{-60}{\celsius} and the minimum near \SI{-80}{\celsius}, supporting the carrier-trapping picture in which trapped carriers are unavailable to quench the nucleus. Taken together, these results connect the optical and nuclear observables of $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ through a unified picture of electron defects and Th-related traps, while providing a comprehensive characterization of the material relevant to solid-state nuclear clock operation.

AI.tldr: Temperature-dependent luminescence study of $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ resolves STE thermal quenching, eleven thermoluminescence glow peaks, and afterglow components; trap depths correlate with isomer quenching, unifying optical and nuclear observables for solid-state nuclear clock operation.
AI.motivation: $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ is a leading solid-state nuclear clock candidate due to the low isomer transition energy (8.3557 eV) and high CaF$_2$ bandgap (~12 eV). Understanding how temperature-dependent carrier trapping affects isomer quenching is essential for clock operation, yet the optical and nuclear observables had not been connected in a unified picture.
AI.method: Synchrotron x-ray excitation combined with a cryo-vacuum system was used to perform temperature-dependent luminescence measurements on $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$, covering radioluminescence, photoluminescence, thermoluminescence, and afterglow. The STE scintillation thermal quenching was resolved into triplet and singlet components; eleven thermoluminescence glow peaks and their emission bands were identified; and long-lived afterglow components were separated.
AI.result: The self-trapped exciton scintillation thermal quenching was resolved into triplet and singlet components. Eleven thermoluminescence glow peaks with associated emission bands were identified, and temperature-dependent afterglow components were separated. Trap depths derived from these measurements closely correlate with the temperature dependence of x-ray-induced isomer quenching, including enhanced isomer yield near -60 °C and a minimum near -80 °C.
AI.conclusion: The results support a carrier-trapping picture in which trapped carriers are unavailable to quench the nucleus, connecting optical and nuclear observables of $^{229}$Th:CaF$_2$ through a unified picture of electron defects and Th-related traps. This provides comprehensive material characterization relevant to solid-state nuclear clock operation.

title: Weyl superconductivity from Feshbach resonance in the three-dimensional repulsive Hubbard model
summary: Motivated by the first experimental realization of the antiferromagnetic phase transition in the three-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model, we present a theoretical study of the model's 3D superconducting phase. By formulating a 3D extension of the Feshbach mechanism, we provide a unified microscopic picture at strong coupling in which pairing is driven by near-resonant bound states of dopants. These long-lived bound states acquire a qualitatively different internal structure in three dimensions compared to their two-dimensional counterparts, giving rise to a distinct superconducting state, namely a time-reversal symmetry breaking $d_{x^2-y^2}+id_{z^2}$ pairing state. We also provide an estimate of the corresponding critical temperature, and provide evidence that the resulting superconducting phase hosts gapless Weyl points. Our results represent a new milestone for the field of quantum simulation, challenging experiments and large-scale numerics alike to test our predictions.

AI.tldr: This theoretical work extends the Feshbach mechanism to three dimensions to describe superconductivity in the 3D Fermi-Hubbard model, predicting a time-reversal symmetry breaking $d_{x^2-y^2}+id_{z^2}$ pairing state with gapless Weyl points.
AI.motivation: Motivated by the first experimental realization of the antiferromagnetic phase transition in the 3D Fermi-Hubbard model, the authors seek to theoretically characterize the model's 3D superconducting phase.
AI.method: They formulate a 3D extension of the Feshbach mechanism, constructing a unified microscopic picture at strong coupling in which pairing is driven by near-resonant bound states of dopants.
AI.result: The long-lived bound states acquire a qualitatively different internal structure in 3D versus 2D, yielding a distinct time-reversal symmetry breaking $d_{x^2-y^2}+id_{z^2}$ pairing state. They also estimate the corresponding critical temperature and provide evidence that the superconducting phase hosts gapless Weyl points.
AI.conclusion: The results represent a new milestone for the field of quantum simulation, challenging experiments and large-scale numerics alike to test the predictions.

title: Smite: A quasiclassical trajectory (QCT) program for bimolecular collisions and unimolecular dynamics on ab-initio, and machine-learned potential energy surfaces
summary: We present Smite, a Python toolkit for quasiclassical trajectory (QCT) simulations of reactive and inelastic bimolecular collisions, unimolecular dynamics, and molecular collisions with finite surface models. A central feature is the explicit control of reactant preparation: harmonic normal modes admit fixed quantum numbers, prescribed energies, thermal quantum populations, or ground-state Wigner sampling; rotation is prepared at fixed angular-momentum magnitude or from thermal distributions appropriate to diatomic and polyatomic rotors. Rotating-Morse sampling provides a coupled anharmonic treatment of diatomic vibration and rotation, while saved molecular-dynamics phase points provide an alternative source of initial conditions. The same nuclear propagators operate with on-the-fly electronic-structure calculations or user-supplied analytical and machine-learned potential energy surfaces. Additional modules provide constrained rigid-fragment dynamics, thermostat-based preparation, photoionization initial conditions with energy and recoil constraints, and fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH) on multiple PESs with approximate curvature-derived couplings. Geometry optimization, transition-state searches, crossing-point optimization, intrinsic-reaction-coordinate following, and thermochemistry use the same energy and derivative interfaces. Analysis tools connect trajectories to product energy partitioning, stereodynamical correlations, time-resolved vibrational signatures, and independent-atom x-ray scattering.

AI.tldr: Smite is a Python toolkit for quasiclassical trajectory simulations of bimolecular collisions, unimolecular dynamics, and molecule–surface scattering, offering extensive reactant-preparation schemes, flexible potential energy surfaces, and integrated analysis tools.
AI.motivation: QCT simulations require flexible, accurate control over initial conditions and potential energy surfaces, yet existing tools often lack comprehensive reactant preparation and integrated analysis capabilities.
AI.method: The toolkit provides multiple reactant-preparation schemes (harmonic normal modes with fixed quantum numbers, prescribed energies, thermal populations, Wigner sampling; rotational preparation for diatomics/polyatomics; rotating-Morse sampling; saved MD phase points), operates with on-the-fly electronic structure or analytical/ML PESs, and includes constrained dynamics, thermostats, photoionization initial conditions, and FSSH.
AI.result: Smite enables reactive/inelastic bimolecular collisions, unimolecular dynamics, and molecule–surface collisions, with geometry optimization, transition-state and crossing-point searches, IRC following, thermochemistry, and analysis of product energy partitioning, stereodynamics, vibrational signatures, and x-ray scattering.
AI.conclusion: Smite is a unified Python framework combining versatile QCT initial-condition preparation, shared propagator/PES interfaces, and comprehensive trajectory analysis for molecular collision and dynamics studies.

title: Thermal magnon transport in FM/AFM bilayers
summary: Progress in information processing relies on spintronics, where magnetic states serve as efficient carriers for data storage and transfer. In this work, we theoretically study magnon propagation in a bilayer composed of a ferro-magnet and an antiferromagnet. For this purpose, we probe the spin Seebeck effect by introducing a spatially varying temperature profile. This generates a local magnon excitation and a continuous magnon flux from hot to cold regions which we quantify through the resulting non-equilibrium magnon accumulation. Based on the chirality of these modes, we identify specific constraints for magnon modes traveling either from the ferromagnet into the antiferromagnet or vice versa. A key finding is the observation of a thermally triggered spin current in the antiferromagnet, a phenomenon typically absent in bulk antiferromagnets that obey time-reversal symmetry. These results provide important insights into the design of heterostructures for magnonic chirality-selective spin transport.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies magnon propagation in a ferromagnet/antiferromagnet bilayer driven by a thermal gradient (spin Seebeck effect), revealing chirality-based constraints on magnon transmission and a thermally triggered spin current in the antiferromagnet.
AI.motivation: Spintronics relies on magnetic states as efficient carriers for data storage and transfer, motivating the need to understand and control magnon transport in hybrid magnetic heterostructures.
AI.method: A spatially varying temperature profile is introduced to probe the spin Seebeck effect, generating local magnon excitation and a continuous magnon flux from hot to cold regions, quantified via non-equilibrium magnon accumulation. Magnon modes are analyzed with respect to their chirality.
AI.result: Specific chirality-based constraints are identified for magnon modes traveling from ferromagnet to antiferromagnet and vice versa. A thermally triggered spin current is observed in the antiferromagnet, a phenomenon typically absent in bulk antiferromagnets obeying time-reversal symmetry.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide important insights for designing heterostructures for magnonic chirality-selective spin transport.

title: Spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov self-interacting processes
summary: We develop a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains, whose dynamics depends on the past through state- and jump-dependent empirical observables. We demonstrate that a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, reducing the Feynman--Kac equation for occupation and flux statistics to an eigenvalue problem for a new tilted operator coupled to Hamilton--Jacobi characteristics. This provides a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations in a broad class of non-Markovian systems. We illustrate our general results with a bistable self-induced East model.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains with history-dependent dynamics, using a multiscale WKBJ Ansatz to reduce the Feynman-Kac equation to an eigenvalue problem for a tilted operator coupled to Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics.
AI.motivation: Dynamical large deviation theory is well established for Markovian systems, but non-Markov processes whose dynamics depends on the past via state- and jump-dependent empirical observables lack an efficient spectral framework. Existing approaches are computationally costly or inapplicable, motivating a tractable method for quantifying fluctuations in broad non-Markovian systems.
AI.method: Develops a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains whose dynamics depends on past history through state- and jump-dependent empirical observables. A multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, reducing the Feynman-Kac equation for occupation and flux statistics to an eigenvalue problem for a new tilted operator coupled to Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics.
AI.result: The WKBJ-based reduction yields a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations in a broad class of non-Markovian systems. The general results are illustrated with a bistable self-induced East model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed spectral theory provides an efficient and general route to dynamical large deviations in non-Markov processes with memory, with the tilted-operator eigenvalue problem and Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics capturing the interplay of fast configurational relaxation and slow memory evolution.

title: First-Principles Study of Two-Dimensional CeN: Interplay between Structural Stability, Electronic Structure, and Magnetism
summary: In this work, the structural stability, and the electronic and magnetic properties of a novel CeN monolayer derived from the (111) surface of bulk rock salt CeN are investigated using first-principles calculations. Dimensional reduction produces substantial changes in the local atomic environment, decreasing the Ce-N coordination from sixfold in the bulk to threefold in the monolayer and shortening the Ce-N bond length, while preserving an essentially planar hexagonal structure. Moreover, the electronic and magnetic properties are significantly modified, which may be useful for practical applications. Both ferromagnetic (FM) and antiferromagnetic (AFM) configurations were investigated and found to be strongly bound, with the FM state slightly lower in energy. The magnetic moments are predominantly localized on the Ce atoms and mainly originated from the Ce 4f states. The electronic structure also exhibits a pronounced dependence on magnetic ordering, highlighting the connection between localized 4f states and the spin-dependent electronic properties of the system. In addition, the calculated elastic properties confirm the mechanical stability of the monolayer, while phonon calculations support its dynamical stability. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations further indicate that the two-dimensional structure preserves its integrity under finite-temperature conditions. Overall, these results demonstrate that dimensional reduction significantly modifies the structural, electronic, and magnetic behavior of CeN without compromising the stability of the resulting two-dimensional lattice. The combination of structural robustness, localized Ce 4f magnetism, and spin-dependent electronic properties make the CeN monolayer an interesting system for further exploration in two-dimensional magnetism and spin-dependent applications.

AI.tldr: First-principles study of a novel CeN monolayer derived from the (111) surface of rock salt CeN reveals that dimensional reduction lowers Ce–N coordination from sixfold to threefold, shortens Ce–N bonds, and strongly modifies electronic and magnetic properties while retaining mechanical, dynamical, and thermal stability.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to explore how dimensional reduction from bulk rock salt CeN to a two-dimensional monolayer alters the structural, electronic, and magnetic behavior, and whether the resulting monolayer could be a viable system for two-dimensional magnetism and spin-dependent applications.
AI.method: First-principles calculations were used to assess structural stability, electronic structure, and magnetic properties. Ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations were compared. Mechanical stability was evaluated via elastic properties, dynamical stability via phonon calculations, and finite-temperature integrity via ab initio molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: The monolayer adopts an essentially planar hexagonal structure with threefold Ce–N coordination and shortened Ce–N bonds. Both FM and AFM states are strongly bound, with FM slightly lower in energy. Magnetic moments are predominantly localized on Ce atoms and mainly arise from Ce 4f states. The electronic structure shows pronounced dependence on magnetic ordering. Elastic and phonon calculations confirm mechanical and dynamical stability, and AIMD indicates structural integrity at finite temperature.
AI.conclusion: Dimensional reduction substantially modifies the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of CeN without compromising the stability of the 2D lattice. The combination of structural robustness, localized Ce 4f magnetism, and spin-dependent electronic properties makes the CeN monolayer an interesting candidate for further exploration in two-dimensional magnetism and spin-dependent applications.

title: $μ$SR measurements of 3D Ising ferromagnetism in bulk Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ crystals
summary: Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ is a quasi-two-dimensional itinerant ferromagnet with a van-der-Waals layered structure that exhibits substantial magnetic anisotropy. In bulk samples, this material becomes magnetically ordered below 220~K, while in thin samples, the gate-tunability of the ferromagnetic moment has attracted significant interest. Alongside high-temperature ferromagnetism, a low-temperature magnetic state occurs whose nature has not been conclusively identified, with some studies suggesting a transition between ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism with temperature. Here we present magnetometry and $μ$SR data that demonstrate that Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$ exhibits three-dimenional Ising-like ferromagnetism over the entire temperature range between $T_{C}=220$~K and 2~K. The feature at 170~K that has previously been proposed to be a transition to antiferromagnetism is instead likely to represent a domain-freezing transition.

AI.tldr: Magnetometry and μSR data show Fe₃GeTe₂ is a 3D Ising-like ferromagnet from T_C = 220 K down to 2 K; the 170 K feature is a domain-freezing transition, not a ferromagnetism-to-antiferromagnetism crossover.
AI.motivation: Fe₃GeTe₂ is a quasi-2D itinerant van-der-Waals ferromagnet with strong magnetic anisotropy, ordered below 220 K in bulk and gate-tunable in thin samples. A low-temperature magnetic state exists whose nature is unresolved, with some studies proposing a temperature-driven ferromagnetism-to-antiferromagnetism transition; this work aims to identify that state conclusively.
AI.method: Magnetometry combined with muon spin relaxation (μSR) measurements across the full temperature range from T_C = 220 K to 2 K.
AI.result: The material exhibits three-dimensional Ising-like ferromagnetism over the entire temperature range between 220 K and 2 K. The feature at 170 K previously attributed to a transition to antiferromagnetism is instead likely a domain-freezing transition.
AI.conclusion: The low-temperature magnetic state of Fe₃GeTe₂ is not antiferromagnetic; ferromagnetic order persists from T_C = 220 K down to 2 K, so the 170 K anomaly is reinterpreted as domain freezing rather than a magnetic phase transition.

title: Atomic-Scale Imaging of Lattice Relaxation and Topological Flat Bands in Helical Trilayer Graphene
summary: Helical trilayer graphene (HTG) has emerged as a highly tunable moire quantum material that hosts strong electronic correlations and nontrivial band topology. However, the atomic-scale lattice structure and local electronic properties have remained largely unexplored. Here we present a comprehensive real-space study of HTG using a combination of scanning near-field optical microscopy and low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. We directly image supermoire lattice relaxation, revealing large triangular domains separated by sharp domain walls, as well as stripe domains connected by smoothly varying boundaries. Atomic-scale spectroscopy uncovers flat bands with a honeycomb electronic texture and one-dimensional boundary states confined to domain walls. By systematically varying the twist angle, we identify a magic angle of approximately 1.9°, substantially larger than the 1.6 degree predicted by theory. Our results establish a direct microscopic link between lattice relaxation and flat bands in HTG.

AI.tldr: Real-space study of helical trilayer graphene (HTG) using scanning near-field optical microscopy and low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy reveals supermoire lattice relaxation with triangular and stripe domains, flat bands with honeycomb electronic texture, one-dimensional boundary states at domain walls, and a magic angle of approximately 1.9 degrees, larger than the theoretically predicted 1.6 degrees.
AI.motivation: Helical trilayer graphene (HTG) is a highly tunable moire quantum material hosting strong electronic correlations and nontrivial band topology, yet its atomic-scale lattice structure and local electronic properties have remained largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors performed a comprehensive real-space study of HTG combining scanning near-field optical microscopy and low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy, systematically varying the twist angle.
AI.result: Supermoire lattice relaxation was directly imaged, revealing large triangular domains separated by sharp domain walls and stripe domains connected by smoothly varying boundaries. Atomic-scale spectroscopy uncovered flat bands with a honeycomb electronic texture and one-dimensional boundary states confined to domain walls. A magic angle of approximately 1.9 degrees was identified, substantially larger than the 1.6 degrees predicted by theory.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a direct microscopic link between lattice relaxation and flat bands in HTG.

title: Strong Dimerization and Field-Induced Reconstruction of the Low-Energy Spectrum in $\mathrm{Cu}_3(\mathrm{OH})_4(\mathrm{HCO}_2)_2$
summary: We investigate the field-dependent low-energy thermodynamics of the distorted triangular quantum antiferromagnet $\mathrm{Cu}_3(\mathrm{OH})_4(\mathrm{HCO}_2)_2$ using a sector-resolved Superblock Diagonalization Method (SBDM) supplemented by a transfer-matrix treatment of weakly coupled layers. The strong exchange hierarchy, dominated by the Cu1--Cu1 intradimer coupling $J_2=150\,\mathrm{K}$, separates a high-energy dimer sector from a much softer magnetic manifold formed predominantly by the Cu2 moments. In the 24-site cluster, sixteen Cu1 spins form the strongly bound sector while eight Cu2 spins remain magnetically active; polarization of these eight spins gives $S^z=4$ compared with $S^z_{\rm sat}=12$, providing a direct microscopic origin for the one-third magnetization scale. The finite-temperature thermodynamics reveals a non-monotonic field evolution of the low-energy scale: the dominant $C/T$ feature softens with increasing field, reaches a minimum near the field region around $2\,\mathrm{T}$, and subsequently hardens as the low-temperature magnetization approaches $M_{\rm sat}/3$. Temperature and field sweeps thus expose a common field-induced spectral reconstruction, while the strongly reduced entropy reflects the restricted number of thermally active degrees of freedom below the dimer excitation scale. Our results identify strong-dimer-induced reduction of the active magnetic Hilbert space, followed by field-driven reorganization of the residual spin sector, as the common microscopic origin of the one-third magnetic response and the non-monotonic low-temperature thermodynamics.

AI.tldr: Using a sector-resolved Superblock Diagonalization Method with a transfer-matrix treatment, the low-energy field-dependent thermodynamics of the distorted triangular quantum antiferromagnet Cu3(OH)4(HCO2)2 is shown to arise from strong Cu1-Cu1 dimerization that leaves only eight Cu2 spins magnetically active, yielding an S^z = 4 ground-polarized state (versus S^z_sat = 12), a one-third magnetization plateau, and a non-monotonic low-energy scale that softens to a minimum near 2 T before hardening.
AI.motivation: The one-third magnetization response and the unusual low-temperature thermodynamics of the distorted triangular quantum antiferromagnet Cu3(OH)4(HCO2)2 call for a microscopic explanation: how a strong internal exchange hierarchy reorganizes the magnetically active degrees of freedom and produces the observed non-monotonic field dependence.
AI.method: A sector-resolved Superblock Diagonalization Method (SBDM) is applied to a 24-site cluster, complemented by a transfer-matrix treatment of weakly coupled layers. The strong Cu1-Cu1 intradimer coupling J2 = 150 K defines a high-energy dimer sector, and the residual low-energy manifold formed predominantly by Cu2 moments is diagonalized and analyzed via finite-temperature thermodynamics (C/T, magnetization, entropy).
AI.result: In the 24-site cluster, sixteen Cu1 spins occupy the strongly bound sector while eight Cu2 spins remain active; polarizing these eight spins gives S^z = 4 compared with S^z_sat = 12, accounting for the one-third magnetization scale. The dominant C/T feature softens with increasing field, reaches a minimum near 2 T, then hardens as the low-temperature magnetization approaches M_sat/3. The strongly reduced entropy reflects the limited number of thermally active degrees of freedom below the dimer excitation scale.
AI.conclusion: The one-third magnetic response and non-monotonic low-temperature thermodynamics share a common microscopic origin: strong-dimer-induced reduction of the active magnetic Hilbert space, followed by field-driven reorganization of the residual spin sector.

title: Three-Dimensional Topology from Stacking-Controlled Umklapp Scattering in Large-Angle Twisted Graphite
summary: Large-angle twisted graphene lies beyond the local-stacking description of conventional moiré systems: inequivalent rotation centers define distinct commensurate interfaces whose low-energy interlayer hybridization is governed by intervalley Umklapp tunneling. For three-dimensional twisted graphite assembled from interfaces with different crystalline symmetries, a symmetry-constrained effective model reveals that competition between nonchiral and chiral tunneling produces one-ring and two-ring nodal-line phases and a $C_3$-protected higher-order topological insulator in the presence of sublattice (chiral) symmetry. The nodal rings carry integer winding numbers, allowing oppositely wound rings to annihilate into the gapped phase. We further examine how sublattice-symmetry breaking modifies these phases. Density functional theory (DFT) and atomistic calculations for $21.8^\circ$ twisted graphite identify the equilibrium structure as a higher-order topological insulator, while compression drives it into a topological Weyl semimetal phase. These findings establish the stacking sequence of symmetry-inequivalent interfaces as a means of engineering band topology in three-dimensional twisted structures.

AI.tldr: A symmetry-constrained effective model for 3D twisted graphite shows competing nonchiral/chiral intervalley tunneling yields nodal-line and higher-order topological phases, with DFT confirming a higher-order TI at 21.8° that becomes a Weyl semimetal under compression.
AI.motivation: Large-angle twisted graphene exceeds the local-stacking (conventional moiré) description because inequivalent rotation centers create distinct commensurate interfaces whose low-energy interlayer hybridization is controlled by intervalley Umklapp tunneling. The paper aims to understand and engineer band topology in such 3D twisted structures beyond the moiré paradigm.
AI.method: A symmetry-constrained effective model is built for 3D twisted graphite assembled from interfaces with different crystalline symmetries, incorporating competing nonchiral and chiral intervalley Umklapp tunneling under sublattice (chiral) symmetry. The effects of sublattice-symmetry breaking are also analyzed. Density functional theory (DFT) and atomistic calculations are performed for 21.8° twisted graphite, including under compression.
AI.result: The competition between nonchiral and chiral tunneling produces one-ring and two-ring nodal-line phases and a C3-protected higher-order topological insulator when sublattice symmetry is present. The nodal rings carry integer winding numbers, enabling oppositely wound rings to annihilate into a gapped phase. DFT and atomistic calculations identify the equilibrium 21.8° twisted graphite as a higher-order topological insulator, while compression drives it into a topological Weyl semimetal phase.
AI.conclusion: The stacking sequence of symmetry-inequivalent interfaces provides a route to engineer band topology in three-dimensional twisted structures, extending topological design beyond the conventional moiré/local-stacking framework.

title: Entropy-Driven Altermagnetism from Thermal Magnons
summary: We identify a route to altermagnetism driven by entropy upon heating and demonstrate it in a minimal square-lattice antiferromagnet. An exchange modulation is entropically favored because the resulting momentum-dependent magnon splitting increases the magnon entropy, thereby lowering the free energy and favoring altermagnetism. We derive an instability criterion for this exchange-modulated state, predict its temperature-driven reentrant behavior, and show that its overlap with Néel order defines a finite-temperature altermagnetic phase. Variational spin-wave theory, spin--lattice Monte Carlo, and cluster diagonalization establish the entropy-driven instability and its coexistence with magnetic order. The resulting state supports a transverse spin conductivity. The mechanism provides a route to thermally induced altermagnetism in compensated magnets coupled to sufficiently soft physical modes.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an entropy-driven route to altermagnetism, where heating favors an exchange-modulated state in a square-lattice antiferromagnet due to magnon entropy, yielding a finite-temperature altermagnetic phase with transverse spin conductivity.
AI.motivation: Altermagnetism typically requires specific collinear magnetic order and lattice symmetry. The paper aims to show that altermagnetism can emerge thermally, driven by entropy rather than only by ground-state exchange, expanding the mechanisms for realizing this phase.
AI.method: The authors analyze a minimal square-lattice antiferromagnet with exchange modulation. They derive an instability criterion for the exchange-modulated state, use variational spin-wave theory, spin-lattice Monte Carlo simulations, and cluster diagonalization to study the entropy-driven instability and its coexistence with Néel order.
AI.result: An exchange modulation is entropically favored because momentum-dependent magnon splitting increases magnon entropy, lowering free energy and favoring altermagnetism. The state shows temperature-driven reentrant behavior, overlaps with Néel order to form a finite-temperature altermagnetic phase, and supports transverse spin conductivity.
AI.conclusion: Entropy can drive altermagnetism in compensated magnets coupled to sufficiently soft physical modes, providing a route to thermally induced altermagnetism and a finite-temperature altermagnetic phase.

title: Nuclear moments, charge radii, and magnetization distribution parameters of Ag isotopes from laser spectroscopy and \textit{ab initio} electronic-structure calculations
summary: The nuclear electromagnetic moments and mean-square charge radii of several silver (Ag) isotopes deduced from recent laser spectroscopy studies in the mass region $A=$ 96-121 are determined using high-accuracy electronic structure calculations performed in this work. We report hyperfine structure and isotope-shift atomic factors calculated with the relativistic coupled cluster approach, including single, double, triple, and perturbative quadruple excitations, CCSDT(Q). Following a systematic theoretical uncertainty analysis, we show that at the precision now achieved (sub-percent uncertainties in some cases), quantum electrodynamic effects become significant. We also show that the isotope-dependent effect in the hyperfine structure due to the non-point-like nuclear magnetization distribution can be extracted with negligible dependence on the assumed nuclear magnetization model at the present level of precision. This also yields a nuclear magnetic dipole moment that is corrected for the hyperfine anomaly induced by the Bohr-Weisskopf effect. In terms of the nuclear electric quadrupole moments, the uncertainty in the electric-field gradient used to extract the quadrupole moments from laser spectroscopy has also been reduced by one to two orders of magnitude relative to values used in previous studies. Finally, the nuclear charge radii of Ag isotopes are extracted using field- and mass-shift factors from our coupled cluster calculations, and the difference in mean-square charge radii between $^{107,109}$Ag agrees with the value deduced from muonic X-ray spectroscopy.

title: Topological Transverse Transport without a Gap in Critical Topological Flat Bands
summary: Quantized Hall transport is traditionally anchored to a bulk spectral gap, which isolates the occupied subspace and exponentially suppresses thermal deviations. Recently discovered critical topological flat bands (CTFBs) challenge this paradigm: an exactly flat band touches a dispersive continuum while retaining a well-defined integer Chern number. However, their finite-temperature transverse transport properties remain entirely unexplored. Here, we develop a low-temperature theory of the intrinsic electrical, thermoelectric, and thermal Hall responses in CTFBs. At fixed particle number, the macroscopic flat-band degeneracy forces a singular Lambert-$W$ drift of the chemical potential, generating an algebraic-logarithmic hierarchy of low-temperature corrections: $T\ln(1/T)$ for electrical Hall, $T[\ln(1/T)]^2$ for thermoelectric Hall, and $T[\ln(1/T)]^3$ for thermal Hall conductivity, replacing the activated thermal protection of a gapped Chern insulator. By contrast, externally pinning the chemical potential to the flat-band energy locks the flat band to half occupation at any nonzero temperature, obstructing the recovery of the fully filled topological ground state as $T\to0^+$. Our results establish that a bulk spectral gap is unnecessary for zero-temperature Hall quantization, but indispensable for its exponential thermal protection.

title: Nature of the 175-180 cm$^{-1}$ Raman Feature in Altermagnetic $α$-MnTe
summary: The 175 cm$^{-1}$ Raman mode in $α$-MnTe has long been assigned to the material's only symmetry-allowed phonon ($E_{2g}$), yet first-principles calculations consistently place this mode below 100 cm$^{-1}$. Recent works have offered three competing explanations for the discrepancy: a weak symmetry-lowering ($D_{6h}\rightarrow D_{3h}$) phonon, an electronic plasmon arising from intrinsic hole self-doping, or an extrinsic MnTe$_2$ impurity signature. Here we resolve this controversy using stoichiometry-controlled molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). We deliberately vary the fraction of pyrite-type MnTe$_2$ secondary phase relative to the $α$-MnTe matrix. Across this series, the 175 cm$^{-1}$ mode tracks the presence of MnTe$_2$ essentially one-to-one -- present wherever MnTe$_2$ is detectable, absent in stoichiometric, single-phase $α$-MnTe at nominal LASER powers. When LASER power is ramped up, an additional mode emerges in MnTe as well positioned close to $\approx$ 175 cm$^{-1}$; our detailed temperatures dependendent Raman analysis identifies the LASER power scorched region close to a distorted MnTe phase, confirmed via transmission electron microscopy. This direct, growth-controlled correlation identifies the mode as an extrinsic MnTe$_2$ impurity signature or as a distorted MnTe feature, rather than an intrinsic phonon or plasmon feature, providing a practical diagnostic for phase purity in MBE-grown $α$-MnTe and clarifying which Raman features can be reliably attributed to the intrinsic altermagnetic phase.

title: Impurity-induced Friedel oscillations and Wigner crystallization in Luttinger liquids via Unified Field Bosonization Technique
summary: We present an analytical study of impurity-induced density correlations in interacting one-dimensional Luttinger liquids using the Unified Field Bosonization Technique (UFBT). Unlike conventional approaches that treat impurities perturbatively, UFBT incorporates localized impurities exactly at the free-fermion level while treating interactions non-perturbatively. Closed analytical expressions for fermionic Green functions and density-density correlation functions are obtained for strongly inhomogeneous systems, enabling a unified description of the impurity-induced $2k_F$ Friedel oscillations and the $4k_F$ Wigner-crystal like correlations. The corresponding scaling behaviour is derived analytically, revealing a crossover in the dominant long-distance correlations at $g=1/3$: Friedel correlations dominate for $g>1/3$, whereas Wigner-crystal like correlations become dominant for $g<1/3$, corresponding to the regime of sufficiently strong repulsive interactions. A reflection-coupled harmonic analysis is developed to account for the left-right mixing induced by impurity backscattering and to consistently reproduce the resulting density correlations. The spinless limit is also obtained as a direct reduction of the spinful formulation. These results provide an analytically controlled framework for describing impurity-induced and interaction-driven density correlations in strongly inhomogeneous one-dimensional quantum systems.

A framework that treats localized impurities exactly while handling interactions non-perturbatively is needed to describe impurity-induced density correlations across interaction regimes.

title: Long-lived divergence from equilibrium of electrons, nuclear spins and lattice for a solid state ion trap at low temperature
summary: A fundamental problem in physics as well as engineering is equilibration. For example, the regulation of thermal and quantum fluctuations enables thermal and quantum annealing of complex systems. A key question is how different subsystems, such as electrons, nuclear spins and phonons equilibrate on their own as well as with each other. Level crossings play a special role in the dynamics of coupled degrees of freedom, for it is here that entanglement can be maximized to speed up relaxation. Here we use optical methods to establish the electronuclear level scheme, including avoided and unavoided crossings, and to examine equilibration of a rare earth ion (Ho$^{3+}$) in a salt (LiYF$_4$), a model system with quantum fluctuations which can be tuned via an external magnetic field transverse to the crystallographic long axis of the tetragonal host. We track the state of the system by monitoring the populations of the levels as a function of swept longitudinal fields, and discover that at low temperatures, depending on the experimental protocol, vastly different non-equilibrium states arise. We find evidence that nuclear spin excitations diffuse and equilibrate without the assistance of phonons, and tend to acquire higher effective temperatures than the electronic spins and the yet cooler lattice. A theory of thermally assisted tunneling rules out the standard scenario of phonon -assisted tunneling, and instead suggests that fast dynamics at level anti-crossings are facilitated entirely by nuclear spin diffusion. This provides a new understanding of thermalization and related slow relaxation phenomena in dense, multi-component interacting quantum systems.

AI.motivation: Equilibration of coupled subsystems (electrons, nuclear spins, phonons) is a fundamental physics and engineering problem central to thermal and quantum annealing. Level crossings are thought to be key points where entanglement is maximized to accelerate relaxation, but how different subsystems equilibrate with each other at such crossings remains poorly understood. The authors seek a model system with tunable quantum fluctuations to directly probe these dynamics.
